Under N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.1(d), a stage 3 or 4 pressure sore, or multiple stage 2 pressure sores, is a characteristic that permits (but does not require) the facility to move a resident, and any decision to keep or move the resident is documented in the record. A resident with a single stage 2 pressure sore must be retained, with a plan of care. The admission agreement states whether the facility retains residents with these conditions, to what extent, and at what added cost (N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.1(e)). Residents who need specialized long-term care are transferred (N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.1(f)). Turning, positioning and nutrition measures are included in the service plan.

definitions.definition: Damage to skin or underlying tissue caused by pressure, shear or friction, usually over a bony area.
Intact skin with persistent redness that does not blanch.
Partial-thickness skin loss, such as a shallow open area or blister, without deeper tissue exposed.
Full-thickness skin loss (stage 3) or loss with exposed muscle or bone (stage 4).
The written plan of care developed from the RN health care assessment (N.J.A.C. 8:36-7.2(e)).

procedures: At admission, a licensed nurse inspects the resident's skin, with attention to the sacrum, heels, hips, elbows and other bony areas, in privacy and with respect for the resident, and records any open areas, redness or bruising. The RN completes and signs the skin assessment as part of the health care assessment within 14 days of admission (N.J.A.C. 8:36-7.2(c)).

The RN uses a pressure-injury risk screen, such as the Braden Scale or an equivalent tool chosen by the Director of Nursing, at admission, at each reassessment and whenever the resident's condition changes, and records the score.

The RN writes prevention measures in the health service plan (ADM-04): a turning and repositioning schedule, pressure-relieving devices, seating and heel protection, continence care, moisture management, safe transfers to avoid shear, nutrition and hydration goals, and daily skin checks.

Direct-care staff check skin during bathing and dressing every day and report immediately to the RN any redness, blister, broken skin, drainage, odor or pain. They do not treat open areas on their own.

When a skin change is reported, the RN assesses the area within [TIME SET BY DIRECTOR OF NURSING] hours, documents location, size, depth, stage, drainage and surrounding skin, and notifies the physician for any open pressure area. The RN records orders. The family or designee is informed with the resident's consent (HLT-05).
The RN or licensed nurse carries out wound treatments as ordered. Staff do not apply treatments unless the RN has delegated the task under HLT-04 and the task is permitted under N.J.A.C. 13:37.

The RN reassesses and measures each open pressure area at least weekly and whenever it worsens, and records the stage and the response to treatment. The health service plan is updated as the wound changes.
The dietary staff and RN review nutrition and fluid needs for any resident with skin breakdown or high risk, and the plan may include dietitian input, supplements or therapeutic diet orders (DL-01).
Single stage 2 pressure sore: the facility retains the resident and the RN writes a plan of care that lists treatment, pressure relief, monitoring and the date for reassessment.

Stage 3 or 4 or multiple stage 2 sores: the RN notifies the Administrator the same day. The Administrator, RN and physician review whether the facility can safely meet the resident's needs, including the added services and cost described in the admission agreement. The decision to keep or move the resident, and the reasons, are recorded in the resident record under N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.1(d).

If the review concludes that the resident needs specialized long-term care, or that the facility cannot meet the resident's needs, the facility follows ADM-05 and ADM-06. It does not move a resident without notice, the resident's participation and the documented process.

Any pressure sore that develops after admission is reviewed as a possible quality-of-care event. The RN and Administrator check whether prevention steps were followed and record corrective actions (GOV-06). Where the facility suspects neglect, staff follow SAF-01.

The Director of Nursing keeps a monthly list of residents with pressure injuries, by stage and whether the sore was present at admission or acquired in the facility, and reports it to the quality improvement committee.
Skin care, turning and repositioning, and reporting of skin changes are part of orientation and annual in-service training for direct-care staff (STF-03).

responsibilities.duty: Assesses skin at admission and on change of condition, writes the plan, stages and measures wounds, notifies the physician and supervises treatments.
Perform daily skin checks, carry out turning and positioning, and report skin changes immediately.
Reviews retention decisions with the RN and physician, makes sure the admission agreement describes retention and costs, and follows the discharge process when required.
Provide meals and snacks that match nutrition and hydration orders.

documentation: Admission and change-of-condition skin assessments
Pressure-injury risk screen scores
Health service plan with turning, positioning and nutrition measures
Wound assessment and measurement records, treatment orders and physician notification
Documented retention or transfer decision under N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.1(d)
Monthly pressure-injury list and quality improvement committee review

policies.title: Hospice and Home Health Coordination
policies.applies_to: ALR, CPCH and ALP
policies.purpose: To make sure residents who receive hospice or home health services from an outside agency get coordinated, safe and dignified care. The policy defines who provides which care, how the outside agency's plan fits with the facility's service plan, and how retention of residents with higher needs is decided and documented.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides or coordinates personal care and services based on assessment by qualified persons, consistent with the Nurse Practice Act and N.J.A.C. 13:37 (N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.1(a)). Residents may receive hospice or home health services from a licensed outside agency of their choice. The facility will have a written agreement with each outside provider that serves its residents. The agreement states each party's responsibilities, how the parties communicate, and how the two plans of care are kept consistent. The hospice or home health plan is coordinated with the facility Health Service Plan so that no service is duplicated or left unassigned. The facility is capable of nursing services, including for nursing-home-level residents (N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.1(d)). A resident with one or more of the eight characteristics listed in 5.1(d) may, but need not, be moved. If the facility decides to retain the resident, the record documents which characteristic applies and why retention is appropriate. A single stage 2 pressure sore must be retained with a plan of care. Residents who need specialized long-term care must be transferred (N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.1(f)). The admission agreement states whether hospice residents are retained, to what extent, and at what added cost (N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.1(e)). The facility does not require a resident to leave only because hospice has been elected, provided the facility can safely meet the resident's needs with the combined plans.

definitions.definition: A licensed hospice program that provides palliative, comfort-focused care and support to a resident with a terminal illness and to the resident's family.
A licensed outside agency that provides skilled nursing, therapy or aide services to a resident in the resident's unit on a time-limited basis.
The facility Health Service Plan (ADM-04) with the outside agency's plan of care attached or cross-referenced, showing who gives each service, when, and how changes are communicated.

The eight characteristics in N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.1(d): 24-hour nursing supervision; bedridden more than 14 days; totally dependent in 4 or more ADLs; severe cognitive decline; stage 3 or 4 pressure sores or multiple stage 2 sores; needs more than assistance with transfer; danger to self or others; unstable condition.

procedures: Before the facility accepts any resident who is receiving or expects to receive hospice or home health services, the Administrator or designee reviews the facility's service capabilities (GOV-02) and the retention terms in the admission agreement (RR-03, ADM-05) with the resident and representative.

The Administrator or designee executes a written agreement with each hospice and home health agency that serves residents. The agreement covers the agency's responsibility for its own plan of care, staff identification and sign-in, 24-hour contact numbers, medication and supply handling, and notification of changes. The agreement is kept in the Administrator's office. The Administrator reviews it at least annually.

The resident, or the resident's legal representative, chooses the hospice or home health provider. Staff give a list of available agencies if asked. Staff do not steer residents to an agency in exchange for any payment or benefit.
On the day services start, the Registered Nurse (RN) or designee obtains the outside agency's plan of care, orders, contact names and after-hours number. Copies go into the resident record.

Within 3 business days of the start of outside services, the RN convenes a care conference by phone or in person with the outside agency nurse or case manager, the resident and representative, and the direct care supervisor. The conference produces a written division of duties, such as ADL assistance, medication administration, symptom monitoring, dressing changes and equipment, and the resident's wishes.

The RN updates the Health Service Plan (ADM-04) to reflect the division of duties and the hospice or home health plan. The plan states who gives each service. It also states how PCAs report observations to the outside agency and what the PCA does if the agency's staff are not present when a need arises.

Where the resident has one or more 5.1(d) characteristics, the RN documents in the record which characteristic applies and the facility's decision to retain the resident or to transfer. The Administrator signs the decision. Retention is documented only when the combined facility and outside agency services can safely meet the need.
If the resident has a single stage 2 pressure sore, the facility retains the resident and the RN writes a plan of care (HLT-08).

Medications are handled under HLT-02 and HLT-03. Hospice comfort-kit and controlled-substance medications are stored, counted, administered by authorized staff, and disposed of under those policies. Hospice staff do not leave medications unsecured in the unit.

PCAs and certified medication aides work only within the limits of their certification and the RN's delegation (HLT-04). Tasks that require a licensed nurse are done by the RN or by outside agency nurses.

Staff report any change of condition, new symptom or comfort concern to the RN and then to the outside agency per the agreement and HLT-05. The record documents the notification, who was reached and the response.

Hospice and home health staff record each visit in the facility's record or a communication log so that facility staff can see what was done and what changed. Facility staff record the care they provide and their observations on each shift.

The facility supports the resident's end-of-life wishes, advance directives and spiritual and cultural preferences (RR-05). The RN keeps current code status and orders, such as DNR or POLST, on the resident's chart and where staff can find them quickly.

The RN reviews the coordinated plan at least every 30 days while the resident is on hospice or home health, and immediately after any significant change. The RN documents who attended and what changed.
If the resident's needs exceed what the facility can safely provide, the RN and Administrator follow ADM-05 and ADM-06. They do not discharge solely because hospice was elected.
When the resident dies, staff follow HLT-10. When outside services end for any reason, the RN updates the Health Service Plan within 24 hours.

responsibilities.duty: Signs and reviews written agreements with hospice and home health agencies; approves retention decisions; makes sure the admission agreement states hospice retention terms and cost.
Coordinates the outside agency's plan with the facility plan; leads care conferences; documents 5.1(d) retention decisions; updates the Health Service Plan; delegates tasks within scope.
Provides assigned care under the plan and RN delegation; reports changes immediately; follows medication procedures.

responsibilities.role: Outside hospice or home health agency
responsibilities.duty: Provides its own services per its plan of care and the written agreement; communicates changes and visit notes to the facility.

documentation: Written agreement with each hospice and home health agency
Outside agency plan of care, orders and contact sheet in the resident record
Care conference note with the division of duties
Updated Health Service Plan
5.1(d) characteristic retention or transfer decision, signed by the Administrator
Visit notes and communication log entries
30-day plan review notes

policies.title: Death of a Resident and Prompt Notification
policies.applies_to: ALR, CPCH and ALP
policies.purpose: To define what facility staff must do when a resident dies. The policy ensures prompt notification of the physician, the family or designee and the other parties required by law, accurate completion of the record of death, and respectful release of the resident's remains and belongings according to the resident's wishes.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.7(a)8, which requires policies and procedures delineating the responsibilities of the facility's staff in making prompt notification regarding the death of a resident as required by N.J.S.A. 26:2H-5e and N.J.A.C. 8:36-15.7(a). When a resident dies, staff notify the resident's physician, the family or designated person and the other parties required by law or directed by the physician, without delay. The facility completes a record of death in accordance with N.J.A.C. 8:36-15.7. Release of the remains and the resident's belongings follows the resident's documented wishes and applicable law. The facility treats the resident, family and other residents with dignity and sensitivity. Disclosures to family members and others involved in the resident's care or arrangements are limited to what is permitted by 45 CFR 164.510(b) and RR-06. As an internal standard, notification of the physician and family or designee is started immediately after the death is recognized and is not delayed for convenience.

definitions.definition: Notification begun immediately after a death is discovered or pronounced and completed without delay. [AGENCY NAME] sets its own standard of starting calls immediately and completing required notifications as soon as the persons can be reached.
The person the resident named in the admission record or advance directive to be notified, or the legal representative or guardian.
The facility record documenting the death as required by N.J.A.C. 8:36-15.7.
The determination of death by a physician, an authorized nurse, hospice staff, emergency medical personnel or another person authorized by law.

procedures: The staff member who finds a resident without signs of life checks responsiveness, breathing and pulse, and immediately calls the on-duty supervisor or RN. If the resident's code status is unknown or full code, staff call 911 and begin CPR unless a valid DNR or comparable order is on the chart (RR-05). If a valid DNR order is in place, staff do not begin CPR and follow steps 3 onward.
The supervisor or RN confirms the resident's code status from the record, stays with the resident, and notifies the Administrator or on-call administrator right away.

The RN or supervisor arranges pronouncement of death by an authorized person. For a resident on hospice, the supervisor calls the hospice agency's 24-hour number so hospice can pronounce and give direction (HLT-09). If no one is available who is authorized to pronounce, the supervisor calls 911.

The RN or supervisor notifies the resident's attending physician immediately. If the physician cannot be reached, the supervisor leaves a message through the answering service and tries the physician's covering provider. Staff record the time of each attempt.

The RN or supervisor notifies the resident's family or designated person immediately after pronouncement, using the contact on the face sheet. Staff make the call personally, tell the person that the resident has died, and do not leave the news on voicemail. If no one answers, staff keep trying every 15 minutes, use the alternate contact, and document each attempt. If the family cannot be reached, the Administrator decides on further steps, such as asking the police to make a welfare notification.

Staff notify the medical examiner, police or other authorities when required by law or when the physician directs, such as for an unwitnessed, unexpected, suspicious or injury-related death. In that case, staff do not disturb the room and do not release the body until the authority gives permission. They follow SAF-01 and SAF-02 if abuse, neglect, exploitation or an elopement-related event is possible.

The Administrator or designee notifies others as required by law or by contract, such as the resident's NJ FamilyCare MLTSS managed care organization or care manager, hospice, home health agency, pharmacy and any other responsible party. Billing for the resident stops as of the date of death, as stated in the admission agreement (RR-03 and ADM-07).

The RN or supervisor completes the record of death as required by N.J.A.C. 8:36-15.7. It includes the resident's name, date and time of death or finding, circumstances, who pronounced and when, the physician notified, persons notified with date and time of each call, the funeral home and the time of removal, and the disposition of belongings. The person completing it signs and dates it.

Staff follow the resident's documented wishes, including advance directives, any pre-arranged funeral plan and religious or cultural preferences. If the resident left no wishes, the facility follows the instructions of the legal representative or next of kin and applicable law.

Staff release the remains only to the funeral director or other person authorized by law. The supervisor confirms the identity of the funeral director, makes sure the body is identified, and records the time and name in the record. Staff do not release remains to anyone who lacks authority.

The supervisor protects the resident's privacy and dignity during removal. Staff use a discreet route when possible, and they tell other residents sensitively and offer support. The Administrator or social worker (HLT-11) offers grief support and a chance for residents and staff to say goodbye.

Staff inventory the resident's belongings with a second staff member present. They list valuables and the contents of the resident's funds account (RR-04) and secure them. The Administrator releases belongings and any funds only to the executor, administrator of the estate, legal representative or other person with legal authority, and obtains a signed receipt.
Medications are removed, counted and disposed of under HLT-02, with a second witness. Controlled substances are documented per that policy.
The Administrator updates the resident's record status, removes the resident from the census and meal and activity lists, and follows RR-03 for any refund of fees or deposits due.

The Administrator reviews the death within 1 business day. If the death was unexpected or followed a fall, medication event, elopement or other incident, the Administrator starts the review in SAF-02 and refers it to the quality improvement program (GOV-06).
Resident records of the deceased are closed and retained under REC-01. Release of any records to family or others follows RR-06 and requires proper authority.

responsibilities.duty: Checks the resident, calls the supervisor or RN, begins CPR unless a valid DNR is on the chart, and stays with the resident.
Confirms code status, arranges pronouncement, notifies the physician and family or designee, completes the record of death, and manages removal and the belongings inventory.
Makes required notifications to others, authorizes release of belongings to legal parties, directs follow-up reviews and ensures staff are trained on this policy.
Supports family, residents and staff; helps locate family or funeral arrangements when requested.

documentation: Record of death (N.J.A.C. 8:36-15.7)
Notification log with each person called, date, time and outcome
Nursing note describing circumstances and pronouncement
Physician or hospice pronouncement documentation
Belongings inventory and signed release receipt
Funeral home release record
Incident report and review, if applicable

policies.title: Social Work Services and Respite Care (if offered)
policies.applies_to: ALR, CPCH and ALP (respite section applies only if [AGENCY NAME] offers respite care)
policies.purpose: To describe how [AGENCY NAME] provides social work services to residents and, if the governing body elects to offer it, short-term respite care. This ensures that residents' psychosocial needs are met and that respite residents receive the same assessment, service planning and rights as long-term residents.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is capable of providing social work services as one of the core services required of an assisted living facility (N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.1(b)). Social work services are provided by a person who meets the qualifications in N.J.A.C. 8:36-13 and who performs the functions that subchapter requires. Social work services support admission and adjustment, psychosocial assessment, family communication, advocacy, referral to community resources, grievance support, grief and loss support, and help with transfers or discharges. Respite care is offered only if the governing body approves it and the facility meets N.J.A.C. 8:36-20, which covers its purpose and scope, policies and procedures, and staffing. If respite is offered, respite residents receive the same assessment, Health Service Plan and rights as other residents. The Administrator reviews the current text of subchapters 13 and 20 at each annual manual review (GOV-05) and updates this policy accordingly.

definitions.definition: Services that address a resident's psychosocial needs, including counseling, referral, family contact, advocacy and discharge planning, provided by a person who meets N.J.A.C. 8:36-13.
Short-term, temporary residence in the facility to give a caregiver relief, provided only if [AGENCY NAME] has elected to offer it under N.J.A.C. 8:36-20.
A person admitted for a defined short stay under a written respite agreement.

procedures: The Administrator designates a qualified social worker or social work provider, employed or under contract, as [SOCIAL WORK DESIGNEE]. The Administrator verifies and files the person's credentials against N.J.A.C. 8:36-13 and STF-05 before the person starts.

The social work designee meets each new resident, and the family or representative where appropriate, within a week of admission to learn about the resident's history, supports, preferences and concerns. The designee records the contact in the resident record.

The social work designee contributes psychosocial information to the admission assessment and reassessments (ADM-03) and to the Health Service Plan (ADM-04), including adjustment, mood, cognition-related concerns, social connections and family involvement.

The designee follows up with the resident after any significant change, such as a hospitalization, loss of a spouse, a roommate change, or a change in care level. The designee documents the follow-up.

The designee refers residents to community resources, including mental health providers, ombudsman, benefits counselors, transportation services and NJ FamilyCare MLTSS care managers. The designee records each referral and its outcome.
The designee helps residents and families raise concerns and use the grievance process (RR-02) and gives information about the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman.
The designee takes part in discharge, transfer and relocation planning (ADM-06) and supports residents and families through the process.
The designee provides or arranges grief support after a death (HLT-10) for residents, families and staff.

If the governing body decides to offer respite care, it records the decision in its minutes. The Administrator then adopts a written respite procedure that follows N.J.A.C. 8:36-20 and states who may be admitted, the maximum length of stay, the fee, and how care is staffed.

Before a respite stay, staff complete pre-admission screening (ADM-01), confirm the person's needs fall within the services the facility can provide (GOV-02 and ADM-05), and obtain a physician's information and orders and the health documentation the facility requires for admission.

The respite resident and representative sign a written respite agreement that states the dates of the stay, the fee, the services provided, the policy on medications, and what happens if the person's needs exceed the facility's capabilities or the person wishes to remain longer.

The RN completes an assessment within the time required for admissions (ADM-03) and writes a Health Service Plan (ADM-04) for each respite resident. Respite residents are given the resident rights notice (RR-01) and the grievance procedure (RR-02).
Medications of respite residents are managed under HLT-02 and HLT-03. Staff secure and inventory the person's own supplies at the start of the stay and return them at the end.
The Administrator makes sure staffing on respite days meets STF-01 and the staffing requirement in N.J.A.C. 8:36-20, based on the acuity of all residents including respite residents.

At the end of a respite stay, staff return belongings and medications, give the person and family a written summary of care and any follow-up needs, and update the census. If the person wishes to stay, the facility follows regular admission procedures.
The Administrator reviews social work and respite activity as part of quality improvement (GOV-06) at least annually.

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether to offer respite care and approves the respite procedure.
Designates and verifies the social worker, ensures staffing, keeps this policy aligned with N.J.A.C. 8:36-13 and 8:36-20, and reviews the program annually.
Performs psychosocial assessments, follow-up, referrals and support, and documents each contact.
Assesses respite residents and writes their Health Service Plans.

documentation: Social worker credentials and contract or job description
Social work contact notes in the resident record
Referral log with outcomes
Governing body minutes approving respite (if offered)
Respite agreement, assessment and Health Service Plan for each respite resident
Annual review notes

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: ALR, CPCH and ALP
policies.purpose: To protect residents from abuse, neglect, exploitation and misappropriation of property, and to ensure every alleged or suspected case is reported immediately to the Department of Health and, for residents 60 or older, to the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.7(a)4. [AGENCY NAME] has zero tolerance for abuse, neglect, exploitation and misappropriation of resident property. All alleged and suspected cases of resident abuse or exploitation are reported to the Complaints Program of the Division of Health Facility Survey and Field Operations at 1-800-792-9770. If the resident is 60 years of age or older, the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman is also notified at 1-877-582-6995, in compliance with N.J.S.A. 52:27G-7.1 et seq. A suspected case that has been reported to the Ombudsman is also a reportable event under N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.10. The Administrator or designee telephones the Division immediately at (609) 633-9034, or (609) 392-2020 after business hours, and sends written confirmation within 72 hours. For Assisted Living Programs, the same report is made under N.J.A.C. 8:36-23.17(b). Staff report immediately. A report does not need proof. Suspicion is enough, and staff do not wait for the Administrator's approval or for an internal investigation. No one is retaliated against for reporting in good faith. Staff are told that a finding of abuse, neglect or misappropriation may lead to review by the Department, entry on the personal care assistant or medication aide abuse registry (N.J.A.C. 8:36-9.1 and 8:36-9.2), and action against an administrator's certificate (N.J.A.C. 8:36-3.5). Disclosures about suspected abuse are made as permitted by 45 CFR 164.512(c) and RR-06.

definitions.definition: Any willful act or omission that causes or may cause physical, emotional, sexual or verbal harm to a resident, including hitting, rough handling, threats, humiliation, unreasonable seclusion, and sexual contact.
Failure to provide the care, supervision, food, medication or services a resident needs to avoid harm.
Improper use of a resident's money, property or identity for another person's benefit, including theft, coercion to sign documents, and misuse of funds.
Reported by anyone or reasonably suspected from observation, injury, behavior or other signs, whether or not it has been proven.
An event that must be telephoned immediately to the Division and confirmed in writing within 72 hours under N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.10.

procedures: Immediate safety. Any staff member who sees or suspects abuse, neglect or exploitation first makes sure the resident is safe. If anyone is in immediate danger or injured, staff call 911 and summon the RN or supervisor. Staff separate the alleged abuser from the resident.

Immediate report. The staff member who observed or learned of the matter reports it at once to the Administrator or on-call administrator. If the Administrator is not reachable or may be involved, the staff member reports directly to the DOH Complaints Program at 1-800-792-9770 without delay. No staff member may be told to wait or to keep silent.

DOH Complaints Program. The Administrator or designee calls 1-800-792-9770 immediately after learning of any alleged or suspected abuse or exploitation, and records the date, time, name of the person spoken to and any reference number.
Ombudsman. If the resident is 60 or older, the Administrator or designee also calls the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman at 1-877-582-6995 immediately and records the call.

Reportable event call. Because the suspected abuse has been reported to the Ombudsman, the Administrator or designee also telephones the Division of Health Facility Survey and Field Operations at (609) 633-9034, or (609) 392-2020 after business hours, immediately (SAF-02). For an Assisted Living Program, the call is made under N.J.A.C. 8:36-23.17(b).
Written confirmation. The Administrator sends written confirmation to the Division within 72 hours of the telephone report and keeps a copy and proof of delivery.

Law enforcement. If a crime may have occurred, the Administrator or the supervisor also notifies law enforcement and follows its direction. Staff do not interview or confront the alleged abuser in a way that could interfere with a criminal investigation.

Medical care. The RN assesses the resident, arranges medical care as needed (HLT-05), and documents injuries objectively, with body diagrams and photographs when the resident or representative consents and policy permits. Staff preserve clothing, linens and other evidence.

Protection of the resident and others. The Administrator immediately removes any employee, volunteer or contractor who is alleged to have caused harm from contact with residents. Removal lasts until the investigation is complete. If the alleged abuser is a resident, staff separate the residents, assess both, and revise the service plans (ADM-04).

Notification of family. With the resident's consent, the Administrator notifies the family, guardian or designated person promptly (SAF-02), unless that person is the alleged abuser. In that case the Administrator notifies another contact and the authorities.

Investigation. The Administrator begins an internal investigation within 24 hours. It includes statements from the resident, witnesses and the accused, review of schedules, and review of records. The Administrator cooperates fully with the Department, the Ombudsman and law enforcement. The investigation is completed and documented in 5 business days unless the authorities direct otherwise. The Administrator does not delay reports until it is finished.

Outcome. If the allegation is substantiated, the Administrator takes corrective action, including termination of employment where warranted. The Administrator also cooperates with the Department's review of personal care assistant or medication aide findings, including registry entry and hearing rights under N.J.A.C. 8:36-9.1 and 8:36-9.2. The Administrator understands that findings of abuse, neglect or misappropriation can lead to action on an administrator certificate under N.J.A.C. 8:36-3.5.

Prevention and training. At hire (before unsupervised resident contact) and at least annually, every employee, volunteer and contractor is trained on recognizing and reporting abuse, neglect and exploitation, on the phone numbers in this policy, and on the non-retaliation rule (STF-03). Training records are kept in the personnel file.
Screening. The facility performs background checks and registry checks before hire and for renewals (STF-02, STF-05). The facility does not employ anyone with a disqualifying finding.

Posting. The numbers 1-800-792-9770 and 1-877-582-6995 are posted in the lobby, on every nursing and care station and in the staff room, and given to residents with the rights notice (RR-01 and RR-02).

Non-retaliation. The Administrator makes sure no resident or staff member is discharged, disciplined, harassed or treated differently for reporting in good faith. Any retaliation is itself grounds for discipline up to termination.

Review. The Administrator reports every case, with its outcome, to the quality improvement committee within 30 days (GOV-06). The committee looks for patterns and recommends changes in training, staffing or supervision.

responsibilities.duty: Protect residents, report any suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation immediately, and cooperate with investigations.
Makes all required calls and written confirmations, removes alleged abusers from contact, leads the investigation, ensures training and posting, and protects reporters from retaliation.
Assesses and treats the resident, documents injuries and preserves evidence.
Receives reports of substantiated cases and ensures resources for prevention.

documentation: Incident and allegation report
Log of calls to DOH Complaints Program, Ombudsman and Division (date, time, person reached)
Written confirmation sent within 72 hours, with proof of delivery
Investigation file and outcome
Nursing assessment and injury documentation
Training attendance records
Registry and background check records
Quality improvement committee minutes

policies.title: Incident, Accident and Reportable Events Reporting
policies.applies_to: ALR, CPCH and ALP
policies.purpose: To ensure every incident, accident and event that must be reported to the Department of Health or to families is identified, documented, reported on time and reviewed.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.10(a) and, for Assisted Living Programs, N.J.A.C. 8:36-23.17(b). [AGENCY NAME] notifies the Division of Health Facility Survey and Field Operations immediately by telephone at (609) 633-9034, or at (609) 392-2020 if after business hours. Written confirmation follows within 72 hours. The reportable events under 5.10 are: (1) termination of the administrator, with the replacement's name and qualifications; (2) any elopements; and (3) any suspected cases of resident abuse or exploitation that have been reported to the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman. Assisted Living Programs also report reportable infections and diseases among residents under N.J.A.C. 8:57 and suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation reported to the Ombudsman, as listed in 23.17(b). With the resident's consent, the facility promptly notifies the family, guardian or designated person of any serious accident, criminal act or incident causing serious harm or injury, or the resident's arrest or detention, and also notifies the Certificate of Need and Licensing Program in writing (N.J.A.C. 8:36-23.8 for ALPs; the facility applies the same practice to ALR and CPCH residents under the corresponding ALR notification requirement). Staff are trained to report every incident to a supervisor by the end of the shift, and to treat reportable events as requiring an immediate call.

definitions.definition: Any unusual occurrence involving a resident, visitor or staff member that affects or could affect health, safety or rights, such as a fall, injury, medication error, behavior event, property loss, or arrest.
An event listed in N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.10 (or 23.17(b) for ALP) that must be called in immediately and confirmed in writing within 72 hours.
Use (609) 633-9034 during the Division's business hours and (609) 392-2020 at other times, including nights, weekends and holidays.
The family member, guardian or other person the resident has named to be notified.

procedures: Any staff member who is involved in or sees an incident secures the resident's safety, gets medical help as needed (HLT-05), and reports the incident to the shift supervisor or RN immediately.
The supervisor completes an incident report before the end of the shift. It records who, what, when, where, witnesses, injuries, actions taken and notifications made.
The supervisor tells the Administrator or on-call administrator about any serious event right away, and about all other incidents by the next business morning.

The Administrator decides at once whether the event is reportable under 5.10 (or 23.17(b) for ALP): administrator termination, any elopement, suspected abuse or exploitation reported to the Ombudsman, and for ALPs reportable infections or diseases under N.J.A.C. 8:57. When in doubt, the Administrator reports.

For a reportable event, the Administrator or designee telephones the Division immediately at (609) 633-9034 (business hours) or (609) 392-2020 (after hours). The caller records the date, time, name of the person spoken to and what was reported.
Within 72 hours of the call, the Administrator sends written confirmation to the Division and keeps a copy and proof of delivery.
If the event is the termination of the administrator, the governing body gives the Division the replacement administrator's name and qualifications as part of the report (STF-07).

If the event is an elopement, follow SAF-03. If the event is suspected abuse or exploitation, follow SAF-01, including the call to DOH Complaints Program at 1-800-792-9770 and, when the resident is 60 or older, the Ombudsman at 1-877-582-6995.
For ALPs, the Administrator also reports reportable infections and diseases under N.J.A.C. 8:57 as listed in 23.17(b), and follows SAF-07.

Family notification. With the resident's consent, the supervisor or Administrator promptly notifies the family, guardian or designated person of any serious accident, any criminal act or incident causing serious harm or injury, and the resident's arrest or detention. Staff document who was told, when, and the resident's consent.
For those events, and for the resident's arrest or detention, the Administrator also notifies the Certificate of Need and Licensing Program in writing and keeps a copy.
The RN follows up on resident injury or condition changes (HLT-05) and updates the Health Service Plan (ADM-04) if needed.

Within 5 business days of any serious incident, the Administrator reviews the cause, whether staff acted properly, and what can prevent a repeat. The Administrator records corrective actions and dates.
The Administrator keeps a log of all incidents and reportable events and presents trends monthly to the quality improvement committee (GOV-06).

The Administrator posts the Division numbers (609) 633-9034 and (609) 392-2020 at the administrator's desk, the supervisors' station and the on-call binder. Every shift lead is trained on them at hire and every year (STF-03).

Incident reports are stored in the incident file, not in the resident's clinical record, except for a factual note about the event and care provided. Reports are held confidentially under RR-06 and retained under REC-01.

responsibilities.duty: Report every incident to the supervisor immediately and the same shift.
Provides care, completes the incident report, and alerts the Administrator to serious or reportable events.
Determines reportability, makes the immediate call and the written confirmation, notifies families and CN&L, reviews incidents and keeps the log.
Reports administrator termination and replacement details through the Administrator and reviews incident trends.

documentation: Incident report
Reportable event call log (date, time, number called, person reached)
Written confirmation to the Division with proof of delivery
Family/guardian notification record with resident consent
Written notice to CN&L, where applicable
Incident log and review notes
Quality improvement minutes

policies.title: Elopement and Missing Resident
policies.applies_to: ALR, CPCH and ALP
policies.purpose: To prevent elopements, to locate a missing resident quickly and safely, and to ensure the required reports are made.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] identifies residents at risk of elopement through the assessment and addresses them in the Health Service Plan, consistent with N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.1(a), which requires services based on assessment by qualified persons. Any elopement is reportable to the Division of Health Facility Survey and Field Operations immediately by telephone at (609) 633-9034, or (609) 392-2020 after business hours, with written confirmation within 72 hours (N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.10). When a resident is missing, staff begin a search at once, call 911 on the schedule set in this policy, and notify the family, guardian or designated person. After every event the facility reviews what happened and revises the plan. A resident with decision-making capacity who signs out and leaves on his or her own is not eloped. If staff cannot tell whether a resident left on purpose and safely, they treat the resident as missing.

definitions.definition: A resident who is not able to leave the building or grounds safely leaves without staff knowledge, supervision or permission, or whose whereabouts are unknown and who may be at risk.
A resident who cannot be located and whose absence is not explained by a sign-out, planned outing or known plan.
A resident identified through assessment as having a history of wandering or exit-seeking, cognitive impairment, or other factors that make leaving unsafe.
The facility's internal alert, [CODE NAME], used to summon all staff to search.

procedures: Identification. The RN completes an elopement-risk review at admission, at each reassessment (ADM-03) and after any change of condition. Risk factors include dementia, history of wandering, expressed wish to go home and medications. The RN records the risk level.

Planning. For each at-risk resident, the RN adds interventions to the Health Service Plan (ADM-04), such as more frequent checks, a recent photograph and description in the binder, wearable alerts if used, structured activity, and door alarm checks. Any managed-risk or restrictive measure follows ADM-04 and SAF-04.
Photographs. Staff keep an up-to-date photo and description of each at-risk resident in a binder at the supervisor's desk. The binder is updated at least quarterly and with any change in appearance.

Daily checks. Staff test door alarms and other exit controls according to SAF-09 and record the check. Staff report any malfunction to the Administrator at once and add increased supervision until repair.
Discovery. A staff member who finds a resident missing, or who is told one is missing, immediately calls the shift supervisor and announces the missing resident alert.

Search. The supervisor assigns staff to check the resident's unit, common areas, bathrooms, stairwells, closets, outdoor areas, parking lot and perimeter, and any place where the resident usually goes. Staff check the sign-out log and ask if anyone saw the resident leave. Search teams carry a phone or radio and report back.

Staffing. The supervisor keeps the minimum staffing required by STF-01 on duty, including one awake PCA and one additional employee on premises, and calls in on-call staff for the search. Staff do not leave other residents unsupervised.

911. The supervisor calls 911 immediately if the resident is at high risk, the weather is dangerous, it is dark, or there is any sign of danger. For every other resident, the supervisor calls 911 if the resident is not found within 10 minutes of the alert. The supervisor gives the police the resident's description, clothing, photo, medical conditions and last known location.
Notification. The supervisor notifies the Administrator immediately and the resident's family, guardian or designated person promptly. The RN notifies the physician. Staff record each call.

DOH report. The Administrator or designee telephones the Division at (609) 633-9034, or (609) 392-2020 after business hours, immediately, for every elopement. This is done even if the resident is found quickly. Written confirmation is sent within 72 hours (SAF-02). If a case of abuse or neglect is suspected, follow SAF-01.
Continued search. The Administrator coordinates with police, extends the search area, and arranges for other staff or volunteers as police advise. The search continues until the resident is found.

Return. When the resident is found, staff bring the resident back safely, and the RN performs a full assessment, checks for injury and exposure, and notifies the physician (HLT-05). Staff stay calm and kind and do not scold the resident.

Notification of resolution. The supervisor tells the police, family or designee and the Division (if the reportable-event call was made) that the resident has been found. The supervisor records the time.

Review. Within 3 business days, the Administrator and RN review how the resident left, whether the plan was followed, whether doors and alarms worked, and what should change. They revise the Health Service Plan and take corrective action such as repairs, more supervision or reassessment of whether the facility can still serve the resident (ADM-05).

Drills and training. The Administrator trains all staff on this policy at hire and annually, and runs a missing-resident drill on each shift at least annually. Drill results go to the quality improvement committee (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Assesses elopement risk, writes interventions in the plan, and examines the resident after return.
Leads the search, calls 911 at the required time, notifies family and the Administrator, and keeps minimum staffing.
Know at-risk residents, check exits, report a missing resident immediately and take part in searches.
Makes the Division report and written confirmation, coordinates with police, reviews the event and corrects causes.

documentation: Elopement-risk assessment and Health Service Plan interventions
At-risk resident photo and description binder
Door alarm test log
Missing resident search record with times
911 and family notification record
Division telephone report log and written confirmation with proof of delivery
Post-event review and corrective action
Drill records

policies.title: Restraints and Restrictive Practices
policies.applies_to: Assisted Living Residence (ALR), Comprehensive Personal Care Home (CPCH) and Assisted Living Program (ALP); all residents, all shifts, all staff and contracted staff
policies.purpose: To protect every resident's right to be free from chemical and physical restraints, seclusion and punitive restrictions. To set the only narrow, documented, physician-supervised path by which any restrictive measure may ever be considered, and to meet the standards for the use of restraints in N.J.A.C. 8:36-21 (Quality Improvement, restraints and personal care services) and the home- and community-based settings requirements that apply to NJ FamilyCare MLTSS residents.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is a restraint-free home. Freedom from chemical and physical restraints, and from physical and mental abuse and neglect, is a resident right under N.J.A.C. 8:36-4.1(a), and the facility posts and distributes it (see RR-01). Staff will not use physical restraints, chemical restraints or seclusion for staff convenience, discipline, retaliation or to make up for inadequate staffing. Punitive restrictions are prohibited. These include withholding meals, visits, activities, telephone access, mail or personal belongings, and confinement to a room or apartment. Staff respond to distressed or risky behavior with assessment, person-centered care planning, de-escalation and less intrusive alternatives. A resident who cannot be served safely without restraint is handled under the retention and discharge policies (ADM-05, ADM-06). Any exception is limited to what N.J.A.C. 8:36-21 permits. Before it is used, it requires a written physician order, a nursing assessment, documented alternatives tried, informed consent of the resident or legal representative, a time limit, monitoring and Administrator approval. For residents in NJ FamilyCare MLTSS, any restriction on a resident's rights or freedoms must also meet 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4). That means a specific assessed need, a justification in the person-centered plan, less intrusive methods tried first, informed consent, data collection, periodic review and an assurance that the measure causes no harm. Any use of restraint outside an approved exception is reported as an incident (SAF-02) and reviewed as possible abuse or neglect (SAF-01).

definitions.definition: Any manual method, physical or mechanical device, material or equipment attached to or next to the resident's body that the resident cannot easily remove and that restricts freedom of movement or normal access to his or her body. Examples are wrist or vest ties, belts that cannot be released by the resident, geriatric chairs with locked trays, sheets tucked to prevent rising, and holding a resident in place.
A medication used to control behavior or restrict movement that is not required to treat a diagnosed medical or psychiatric condition and is not part of the resident's standard treatment.
Involuntary confinement of a resident alone in a room, apartment or area from which the resident is physically prevented from leaving.
Any limitation of a right, service, privilege or item used as punishment, retaliation or behavior control.

A device such as a bed assist rail, wheelchair seat belt or lap cushion that the resident requested or that was assessed as improving function or safety. It is not a restraint only when the resident can remove or release it voluntarily and it does not restrict free movement.
An immediate and serious threat of physical harm to the resident or others that cannot be stopped by any less restrictive means.

procedures: Admission: At pre-admission screening and assessment (ADM-01, ADM-03), the RN identifies any history of restraint use, wandering, aggression or fall risk and records what less intrusive approaches have worked. The facility does not accept an applicant who requires restraint to be served safely.

Care planning: The Health Service Plan (ADM-04) lists each resident's triggers, preferences and individualized, least-restrictive interventions for distress, wandering, refusal of care or aggression. Staff review it before providing care.

Prohibited practices: No staff member may tie, belt, lock or hold a resident in a chair, bed, room or apartment, withhold access to a call device, or apply any item that prevents the resident from moving. No staff member may request or administer a medication to control behavior unless the physician has ordered it to treat a diagnosed condition and it is documented in the Health Service Plan.

Assistive devices: Before any bed rail, wheelchair belt or similar device is used, the RN assesses it for entrapment and restriction risk and documents the resident's request or consent and ability to release it. The RN reviews the device at each reassessment and at any change of condition. A device the resident cannot release is treated as a restraint under this policy.

Alternatives first: Before considering any restrictive measure, staff try and document alternatives. These include toileting and hydration schedules, pain assessment, low beds, floor mats, sensor alarms used with the resident's consent, one-to-one companionship, walking programs, activity changes, environmental changes, medication review by the physician and pharmacist, and family involvement.

De-escalation: PCAs and nurses use trained de-escalation, which means calm voice, space, redirection and giving choices. They call the RN for any resident who is escalating. If another resident is endangered, staff separate residents by moving the others away rather than confining the resident in distress.

Emergency protection: If a resident is in imminent danger of harming self or others, staff call 911 and the RN immediately. They use the least physical contact needed for the shortest time to protect people, with no prone holds and nothing that restricts breathing or circulation. Staff never use seclusion. The Administrator is notified at once.

Exception review: If the resident's physician, the RN or a representative proposes any measure that could restrict movement, the RN notifies the Administrator the same day. No measure is started until the Administrator and RN confirm in writing that N.J.A.C. 8:36-21 and, for MLTSS residents, 42 CFR 441.301(c)(4) are met.

Required elements before any permitted use: (a) a written, dated physician order stating the reason, the specific measure and its duration; (b) an RN assessment of the medical symptom or safety risk; (c) documentation of the alternatives tried and why they failed; (d) informed consent from the resident or legal representative after explanation of risks and alternatives; (e) a Health Service Plan revision stating the goal of discontinuing the measure; and (f) for MLTSS residents, notice to the MLTSS care manager.

Monitoring during any permitted use: A licensed nurse or trained PCA checks the resident at least every 30 minutes. Staff release the resident, reposition, toilet, offer fluids and check skin at least every 2 hours. The RN reassesses at least every shift day and the physician reassesses at the interval the physician orders. Each check is documented on the Restrictive Measure Monitoring Record.

Discontinuation: The measure ends when the reason ends, when the order expires or when the resident or representative withdraws consent. If the measure is still needed after the review period, the Administrator and RN decide whether the facility can safely continue to serve the resident and begin ADM-05/ADM-06 steps if it cannot.

Reporting: Any restraint, seclusion or restriction used outside an approved exception is reported to the Administrator within 1 hour and recorded under SAF-02. The Administrator reviews it as possible abuse or neglect. Suspected abuse is reported to the DOH hotline at 1-800-792-9770 and, for residents age 60 or older, to the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman at 1-877-582-6995 (SAF-01).

Resident and family notification: The Administrator or RN informs the resident, guardian or designated responsible individual of any proposed or actual restrictive measure on the same day and explains the right to refuse and to complain to the facility, DOH or the Ombudsman (RR-02).

Training: All staff receive training at hire and annually on resident rights, restraint-free care, de-escalation, dementia communication (HLT-06) and abuse reporting (STF-03). Training is documented in the personnel record.

Quality review: The Quality Improvement Committee (GOV-06) reviews quarterly the number of restraint-related incidents, any exception cases, device use and fall rates. It identifies staffing, training or care-planning corrections and records them in the minutes.

Annual review: The Administrator and RN review this policy at least annually with the Policy and Procedure Manual review (GOV-05). They confirm it still conforms to the text of N.J.A.C. 8:36-21 and current MLTSS requirements, and document the review.

responsibilities.duty: Prohibits restraint, seclusion and punitive restrictions; approves or declines any exception; reviews incidents; ensures training and reporting to DOH and the Ombudsman.
Assesses residents and devices, develops alternatives, obtains physician orders, supervises monitoring, documents, and updates the Health Service Plan.

responsibilities.role: Personal care assistants and direct care staff
responsibilities.duty: Use de-escalation and care-plan interventions, never apply restraints, and report any concern to the nurse and Administrator immediately.
Provides any written order with reason and duration and reviews continued need; reviews psychotropic medication for appropriateness.
Tracks and reviews restraint-related events, devices and alternatives, and recommends corrective action.

documentation: Pre-admission and admission assessment notes on restraint history and behaviors
Health Service Plan with individualized least-restrictive interventions
Assistive device assessment and consent
Physician order, nursing assessment, alternatives-tried record and informed consent (for any approved exception)
Restrictive Measure Monitoring Record
Incident reports and abuse/neglect reports with reporting confirmation
Staff training records and QI committee minutes
Annual policy review record

policies.title: Emergency Preparedness, Disaster Plan and Emergency Medical Services
policies.applies_to: ALR, CPCH and ALP; all residents, staff, volunteers and contracted personnel; all shifts
policies.purpose: To ensure that [AGENCY NAME] has a written, filed and practiced plan for medical emergencies, power failures, fire and natural disasters. The plan protects residents and staff and keeps care, medications and records going during and after an emergency. This policy meets N.J.A.C. 8:36-14.2.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 8:36-14.2. [AGENCY NAME] has developed written emergency plans, policies and procedures for (1) medical emergencies, (2) power failures, (3) fire, and (4) natural disasters. The emergency plans are filed with the Department of Health, and the Department is notified whenever the plans are changed. The procedures specify the persons to be notified, the process of notification and how notification is verified; the locations of emergency equipment and alarm signals; evacuation routes; procedures for evacuating residents; procedures for reentry and recovery; the frequency of fire drills; the tasks and responsibilities assigned to all personnel; and the medications and records to be taken from the facility upon evacuation and returned after the emergency. The plan also serves as the facility's written emergency action plan for employees under 29 CFR 1910.38. For any medical emergency, staff call 911 first and then follow the procedures below. The Administrator reviews and tests the plan at least annually and after any actual emergency or building change.

definitions.definition: The written plan, filed with the Department, covering medical emergencies, power failure, fire and natural disasters, with the specific contents listed in N.J.A.C. 8:36-14.2.
Movement of residents out of a threatened area (horizontal or vertical within the building, or out of the building) to a safe location.
Keeping residents inside the building, in the safest area, when evacuation would be more dangerous than staying.
The steps taken to determine that the building is safe, return residents, medications and records, restore services and review the response.

A portable, labeled kit holding the current resident roster and face sheets, medication administration records, medications as directed in this plan, advance directive and code status copies, contact lists, flashlights and basic supplies.

procedures: Plan development: The Administrator and RN write the emergency plan covering medical emergencies, power failures, fire and natural disasters (such as flood, severe storm, snow or ice, and extreme heat). The plan names the shelter or relocation sites and transportation, and the local office of emergency management and fire department contacts.

Filing: The Administrator files the plan with the Department of Health through the Certificate of Need and Licensing Program (PO Box 358, Trenton NJ 08625-0358, (609) 292-6552), unless the Department directs a different address. The date and proof of filing are kept in the Emergency Plan file.

Changes: When the plan changes, including a change of Administrator, phone numbers, evacuation routes, relocation site or building layout, the Administrator updates the plan and notifies the Department in writing within 30 days. Before any renovation or expansion, the Administrator confirms that plans have been approved by the Department of Community Affairs Health Care Plan Review Unit ((609) 633-8151) and updates routes and diagrams before the changed area is occupied.

Persons to be notified: The plan holds a notification list in this order: 911 as needed; the Administrator [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] at [PHONE]; the RN; the owner or governing body; the local fire department and office of emergency management; residents' guardians, designated responsible individuals and families; physicians and the pharmacy; the MLTSS care managers for NJ FamilyCare residents; and the Department of Health. The list is posted at the front desk and in the go-kit.

Verification of notification: The staff member making notifications records the person called, time, method and what was said, and confirms the person acknowledged the message. If there is no answer, the staff member leaves a message and moves to the alternate contact and tries again in 15 minutes. The charge person checks the log until every required contact is verified.

Medical emergencies: Staff who find a resident who is unresponsive, not breathing, choking, bleeding heavily or showing signs of stroke or heart attack call 911 at once and notify the nurse. They begin first aid, CPR or abdominal thrusts per training, and honor a valid DNR or POLST order (RR-05). As the facility's own standard, at least one employee trained in CPR and choking relief is on duty at all times and an AED is available and checked monthly. The RN notifies the physician and family (HLT-05).

Fire: On fire or alarm, staff follow RACE (Rescue, Alarm, Contain, Evacuate or Extinguish). Staff activate the alarm, call 911, close doors, and move residents away from the fire horizontally to the next fire compartment and then out as directed by the fire department. Details are in SAF-06.

Power failure: Staff check the cause, notify the utility and the Administrator, and use emergency lighting and flashlights, not candles. The RN identifies residents who use oxygen concentrators, electric beds or other powered devices and implements backups. Staff protect refrigerated medications and food, and keep doors and exits secure. If the outage threatens health or safety (heat, cold, loss of fire alarm or sprinklers), the Administrator decides whether to shelter in place or evacuate and arranges a fire watch if the fire alarm is not working.

Natural disasters: The Administrator monitors National Weather Service and local emergency management alerts. Staff move residents away from windows during severe storms, stock water, food, medications and supplies, and follow evacuation orders from local authorities. The Administrator decides on evacuation early enough to move residents with limited mobility.

Evacuation routes and equipment: Posted floor plans in each corridor show evacuation routes, exits, alarm pull stations, fire extinguishers, the AED and the first-aid kit. Staff walk the routes at orientation and during drills. Exits and routes are kept clear at all times.

Evacuation procedure: Each shift has an assigned evacuation leader. The RN keeps an evacuation priority list showing each resident's mobility, equipment and need for assistance. Residents who can walk go first with a staff escort, wheelchair users next, and residents needing carry or transfer assistance last. Elevators are not used in a fire. A roll call against the census is completed at the assembly point and reported to the incoming fire official.

Tasks by personnel: The plan assigns written tasks. The Administrator or senior person on duty commands the response and calls 911. The RN or charge nurse manages medications, records and resident medical needs. PCAs assist and account for residents. Kitchen staff handle food and water supplies. Maintenance staff control utilities, and the front desk handles phones and the visitor log. Staff learn their assignments at orientation (STF-03) and again at least annually.

Medications and records: When evacuating, the RN or designated nurse takes the go-kit, the medication administration records, the resident face sheets and code-status documents, and each resident's medications in labeled containers (or arranges them to follow with the pharmacy), including controlled substances under count and double lock where possible (HLT-02). Staff keep a list of what left the building and who carries it.

Drills: Fire drills follow SAF-06. Staff also conduct at least one drill or tabletop exercise per year on a non-fire scenario (for example power failure, severe weather or relocation). Each exercise is documented and reviewed.

Reentry and recovery: The Administrator allows reentry only after the fire official or authorities declare the building safe. The nurse and maintenance staff check utilities, alarm and sprinkler systems, water and temperature. The RN checks each resident for health changes, reconciles the medications and records returned against the evacuation list, and restores care schedules.

Reporting: The Administrator reports emergencies that affect resident health or safety through the incident process (SAF-02, REC-02), including any evacuation, fire, extended power loss or unexpected death, and notifies families and MLTSS care managers.

After-action review: Within 7 days of any real emergency or exercise, the Administrator holds a debrief with staff, records strengths and problems, corrects the plan and refiles it with the Department if it changes.

Annual review: The plan is reviewed at least annually with the manual review (GOV-05). The review checks contact numbers, relocation agreements, resident needs and staff assignments, and is documented.

responsibilities.duty: Writes, files and updates the plan; notifies the Department of changes; leads the response; assigns tasks; approves evacuation and reentry; reports and reviews every emergency.
Manages medical response, the evacuation priority list, medications, records and the go-kit; assesses residents after the event.
Call for help, assist residents, follow assigned evacuation tasks, and account for residents.
Check emergency equipment, lighting and utilities; shut off or restore services as directed; keep exits clear.
Maintain emergency food and water supplies and food safety during an outage.
Provides resources, relocation arrangements and approval of the plan.

documentation: Written emergency plan with filing date and proof of filing with the Department
Notification of plan changes to the Department
Notification log with verification entries
Posted evacuation floor plans and equipment location list
Evacuation priority list and go-kit inventory
Emergency exercise and drill records
Incident reports and after-action reviews
Annual plan review record
Staff training records on emergency roles

policies.title: Fire Safety, Evacuation and Drills
policies.applies_to: ALR, CPCH and ALP; all residents, staff and visitors; buildings, grounds and all shifts
policies.purpose: To prevent fires, ensure alarms, sprinklers and extinguishers work, ensure staff can protect and evacuate every resident, and meet the licensure requirements for local fire approval and a certificate of occupancy or certificate of continued occupancy.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a fire-safe environment. Portable fire extinguishers comply with NFPA 10, Standard for Portable Fire Extinguishers, 2002 edition (N.J.A.C. 8:36-16.15). The facility holds local zoning, fire, health and building approvals and a certificate of occupancy or certificate of continued occupancy, as required for licensure (N.J.A.C. 8:36-2.4), and admits no resident before written Department of Health approval or a license. Fire drills are held at the frequency set in the facility's emergency plan filed with the Department (SAF-05). At minimum, the facility conducts a drill on each shift every quarter, and more often if the Department, local fire official or the plan requires. Staff are trained in their fire tasks, alarm, sprinkler and extinguisher systems are inspected and tested by qualified persons, and every inspection and drill is recorded.

definitions.definition: The staff fire response sequence: Rescue, Alarm, Contain, Evacuate or Extinguish.
Extinguisher use sequence: Pull, Aim, Squeeze, Sweep.

definitions.term: Certificate of occupancy / certificate of continued occupancy
definitions.definition: The local approval confirming that the building may be occupied for its use, required before licensure.
Continuous patrol of the building by trained staff when the fire alarm or sprinkler system is out of service.
An area separated by fire-rated walls and doors, used for horizontal evacuation.

procedures: Approvals before opening: Before submitting the license application and before any admission, the Administrator obtains the local zoning, fire, health and building approvals and the certificate of occupancy or certificate of continued occupancy, and files copies with the Department (N.J.A.C. 8:36-2.4). Admission does not start until written Department approval or the license is received.

Extinguishers: Maintenance staff install portable extinguishers of the types and locations required by NFPA 10 (2002 edition). Maintenance staff perform a visual check monthly, initialed on the extinguisher tag or log. A qualified contractor performs annual maintenance and required periodic testing. Any extinguisher that is discharged, damaged or overdue is replaced or serviced the same day.

Alarm and sprinkler systems: A licensed fire protection contractor inspects and tests the fire alarm, smoke and heat detectors, sprinklers and emergency lighting on the schedule required by the local fire official and applicable code. Maintenance staff test pull stations and emergency lights monthly. All reports are kept on site.

Impairments: If the alarm or sprinklers are out of service, the Administrator notifies the local fire official and the fire alarm contractor at once, begins a fire watch with trained staff, and keeps the watch until the system is restored and documented.

Housekeeping and hazards: Staff keep corridors, exits and stairs clear, keep fire doors closed and not wedged open, report blocked exits, and store flammables safely. Portable heaters, extension-cord overload and open flames (including candles and incense) are not permitted in the building. Smoking follows SAF-08.

Oxygen safety: The RN identifies residents on oxygen. Oxygen use is signed, and no smoking, open flame or sparking device is allowed within the area of use. Cylinders are secured upright and stored away from heat.

Staff response: On any alarm or sign of fire, staff follow RACE. They rescue residents in immediate danger, activate the alarm and call 911, close doors to contain the fire, and evacuate or use a fire extinguisher only if trained and the fire is small and escape is clear (PASS).

Evacuation: Residents are moved first to the nearest safe fire compartment (horizontal evacuation) and then out of the building if directed. The evacuation priority list in SAF-05 is used. Staff do not use elevators. At the assembly point a staff member completes a census roll call and gives the result to the fire department.

Drill schedule: The Administrator sets a written drill schedule so that each shift conducts a drill at least quarterly, with some drills at night and with varied exit routes. The schedule satisfies the frequency in the filed emergency plan and any higher frequency set by the Department or local fire official.

Conducting drills: The Administrator or designee conducts the drill, sounds the alarm, times the response, observes staff tasks, and checks residents' participation, including residents with dementia (HLT-06) or mobility limits. Each drill is assessed for evacuation time, corridor and exit clear, alarm function and staff performance.

Drill record: Within 24 hours, the Administrator completes the Fire Drill Record. It lists date, time, shift, type of drill, participating staff, residents assisted, evacuation time, problems found and corrective action. Missed or failed drills are repeated within 14 days.
Training: New staff learn alarm and extinguisher locations, RACE and PASS, evacuation routes and their assigned tasks before working alone. All staff repeat the training at least annually (STF-03).

Resident orientation: At admission and at least annually, staff review fire safety, exits and drill participation with residents and tell them what to do on an alarm. Residents' reasonable choices and risk agreements are recorded in the Health Service Plan (ADM-04).

Corrections: Deficiencies found in inspections, drills or by the fire official are logged with the date found, person responsible and date corrected. The Administrator checks the log weekly until all items are closed.
Quality review: The Quality Improvement Committee (GOV-06) reviews drill results, inspection findings and corrective action at least quarterly.
Annual review: The Administrator reviews this policy annually with the manual (GOV-05) and after any alarm response, fire event or building change.

responsibilities.duty: Obtains and keeps local approvals and certificate of occupancy; sets and documents drills; ensures inspections and corrections occur.
Perform and record monthly extinguisher and emergency-light checks; arrange contractor testing; keep exits clear; initiate repairs.
Maintain the evacuation priority list and oxygen-safety measures; oversee resident assistance in drills.
Know and carry out RACE, PASS and assigned evacuation tasks; report hazards at once.
Inspect, test and certify the alarm, sprinkler and extinguisher systems.

documentation: Local zoning, fire, health and building approvals and certificate of occupancy or certificate of continued occupancy
Extinguisher monthly check log and annual service tags and reports
Fire alarm, detector, sprinkler and emergency lighting inspection and test reports
Fire watch logs, when used
Fire Drill Record for each drill and the drill schedule
Staff and resident fire safety training rosters
Corrective action log
Annual policy review record

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control, Immunizations and Resident Needle/Syringe Disposal
policies.applies_to: ALR, CPCH and ALP; all residents, staff, volunteers and contractors; all shifts
policies.purpose: To prevent and control infections and communicable disease among residents and staff, to ensure required resident immunizations are offered and documented, to protect staff from bloodborne pathogens, and to ensure that needles and syringes are stored, used and disposed of safely and lawfully.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 8:36-18.3(a), which requires written policies and procedures to be established and implemented regarding infection prevention and control. [AGENCY NAME] uses standard precautions for all residents, maintains an exposure control plan under 29 CFR 1910.1030, and addresses hand hygiene, personal protective equipment, environmental cleaning, laundry, food handling, isolation and outbreak response, employee health (STF-04) and reporting. The Administrator checks the topic list in N.J.A.C. 8:36-18.3(a)1 through 7 against this policy at each annual review so that no required topic is missing. Under N.J.A.C. 8:36-18.2, annual influenza vaccination is documented for each resident per the ACIP recommendations (8/27/2021) unless contraindicated or refused. Vaccination of accepting residents is completed by November 30 each year. Residents admitted after that date, up to February 1, are vaccinated before or on admission as medically appropriate unless they refuse. Pneumococcal vaccination is documented for residents 65 and older per ACIP (1/28/2011), or is provided or arranged before or on admission unless the resident refuses. This policy meets N.J.A.C. 8:36-18.3(a)8. Needles and syringes that residents use as part of home self-care are disposed of in accordance with N.J.S.A. 2C:36-6.1 and N.J.A.C. 8:43E-7. Needles and syringes that the facility itself stores, uses and disposes of follow N.J.S.A. 26:2H-5.10 et seq., N.J.A.C. 8:43E-7, N.J.A.C. 7:26-3A and 29 CFR 1910.1030, with a record of purchase, storage and disposal.

definitions.definition: Infection control practices applied to all residents regardless of diagnosis: hand hygiene, gloves and other PPE based on anticipated contact, respiratory hygiene, safe injection practices, safe handling of sharps, and cleaning of equipment and environment.

The written plan under 29 CFR 1910.1030 that identifies tasks with exposure to blood or other potentially infectious material and sets methods of protection, hepatitis B vaccination, post-exposure evaluation and training.
Needles, syringes, lancets and other items that can puncture or cut skin and may carry infectious material.
Needles, syringes and lancets that a resident uses for self-care (for example insulin injections or blood glucose testing) in his or her own apartment.
The CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices.

procedures: Infection control coordinator: The Administrator designates the RN as infection control coordinator with training in infection prevention. The coordinator maintains this policy, reviews it annually and reports to the Quality Improvement Committee (GOV-06).

Standard precautions: All staff use standard precautions. They perform hand hygiene before and after resident contact, before food handling and medication administration, after glove removal and after toileting. Staff wear gloves, gowns, masks or eye protection when exposure to body fluids or respiratory secretions is possible. Staff with symptoms of communicable illness are managed under STF-04.
