Environmental cleaning: Housekeeping uses EPA-registered disinfectants per label on high-touch surfaces daily and on bathrooms, spills and equipment as needed. Shared equipment (blood pressure cuffs, glucometers, thermometers, lifts) is cleaned and disinfected between residents (DL-03).

Laundry and waste: Soiled linen is bagged at the point of use, handled with gloves and kept away from clean linen and food areas. Contaminated waste is placed in leak-proof bags or containers and removed under the facility's waste procedures.
Food safety: Dietary staff follow safe temperature, storage, sanitation and illness exclusion practices (DL-01).

Illness and outbreaks: Staff report new fever, cough, vomiting, diarrhea, rash or clusters of symptoms to the RN the same shift. The RN assesses, notifies the physician (HLT-05), and may isolate or cohort residents, restrict visitors and limit group activities. The Administrator reports diseases and outbreaks required to be reported to the local health department and follows its instructions. Reporting is documented, and serious events are handled under SAF-02.

Surveillance: The coordinator keeps a monthly infection log by resident and type of infection and reviews it for patterns, such as respiratory, GI, skin or urinary tract infections, and for staff illnesses.

Influenza vaccine: Each fall the RN offers influenza vaccine to every resident with education on benefits and risks. The vaccination is completed by November 30 for residents who accept. For residents admitted after November 30, up to February 1, the vaccine is given before or on admission as medically appropriate unless the resident refuses. The RN records vaccine date, lot number, site and administrator, or the refusal or medical contraindication, in the Immunization Record.

Pneumococcal vaccine: At admission the RN checks vaccination history for residents 65 and older. If not documented, the RN provides or arranges the vaccine before or on admission per ACIP (1/28/2011) unless the resident refuses, and documents the date or the reason it was not given.

Immunization follow-up: The RN reviews the immunization record at annual reassessment (ADM-03). Residents or representatives may change a refusal at any time, and the RN re-offers vaccine at each season and records the response.

Resident home self-care sharps: For a resident who injects or tests at home, the RN confirms during assessment (ADM-03) that the resident can do so safely and records it in the Health Service Plan. The resident is given an FDA-cleared puncture-resistant sharps container, taught to place used needles, syringes and lancets directly into it without recapping, and to keep it out of reach of others. Staff do not handle loose sharps. When the container is three-quarters full, it is sealed and disposed of in the manner permitted by N.J.S.A. 2C:36-6.1 and N.J.A.C. 8:43E-7. The RN or Administrator records the disposal.

Facility-held needles and syringes: Any needles and syringes the facility itself obtains for authorized licensed-nurse use are stored in a locked area, used only by authorized persons under N.J.A.C. 8:36-11.7 and HLT-03, and discarded at point of use into puncture-resistant containers. The facility keeps a record of purchase, storage and disposal. Disposal is through a regulated medical waste process under N.J.S.A. 26:2H-5.10 et seq., N.J.A.C. 8:43E-7 and N.J.A.C. 7:26-3A.

Bloodborne pathogens exposure control: The Administrator maintains a written exposure control plan under 29 CFR 1910.1030. It lists job categories at risk, engineering controls such as safety needles and sharps containers, work practices, PPE, hepatitis B vaccination offered at no cost, labeling and training. The plan is reviewed annually.

Needlestick or exposure response: A staff member who has a needlestick or splash exposure washes the area at once, reports to the RN and Administrator, and is sent for medical evaluation and follow-up without delay. The incident is documented in a sharps injury log and exposure report kept apart from the personnel file as a confidential medical record.
Training: Staff are trained on infection control, standard precautions, hand hygiene, PPE, sharps and exposure control at hire and at least annually (STF-03). Training is recorded.

Quality review and annual review: The coordinator reports infection rates, vaccination rates and sharps incidents to the QI Committee each quarter. The Administrator reviews this policy annually with the manual (GOV-05) and confirms it covers each topic listed in N.J.A.C. 8:36-18.3(a)1 through 7 as currently adopted.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures this policy and the exposure control plan are implemented, resources provided, outbreaks reported, and annual review completed.
Offers and documents vaccines, assesses residents with infection signs, maintains infection log, oversees sharps handling and teaches residents.
Follow standard precautions, handle linen, waste and sharps safely, and report illness and exposures.
Use and keep sharps containers as taught and tell staff when containers are nearly full.
Order and advise on vaccines, treatment and antimicrobial use.

documentation: Written infection prevention and control policy and annual review record
Exposure control plan and staff training records
Resident Immunization Record (influenza and pneumococcal dates, lot numbers or refusals and reasons)
Infection surveillance log and outbreak records
Sharps container issue and disposal records for resident self-care
Facility record of purchase, storage and disposal of needles and syringes
Sharps injury and exposure reports (confidential)
QI committee minutes on infection control

policies.title: Smoking Control, Visitors and Pets
policies.applies_to: ALR, CPCH and ALP; all residents, visitors, staff, volunteers, vendors and animals on the premises
policies.purpose: To control smoking in line with New Jersey law and protect residents from fire and smoke, to welcome visitors while protecting residents' rights, privacy and safety, and to allow pets only with safeguards so that they do not interfere in residents' lives.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 8:36-6.1(a)8, the control of smoking in the facility in accordance with N.J.S.A. 26:3D-55 et seq. and N.J.A.C. 8:6. Smoking, including e-cigarettes and vaping, is not permitted indoors in the building. It is allowed only in a designated outdoor smoking area, if the facility has one, which is posted and kept away from entrances, windows, air intakes and oxygen use. Staff and visitors follow the same rules. [AGENCY NAME] discloses this policy to applicants before admission (ADM-01, RR-03). Residents may receive visitors consistent with the resident rights posted and distributed under N.J.A.C. 8:36-4.1(a) (RR-01). Visitors sign in for safety and security, and the facility restricts a visit only to protect the resident or others, for infection control, or at the resident's request. Under N.J.A.C. 8:36-17.3(b)7, if pets are allowed, the facility provides safeguards to prevent interference in residents' lives. [AGENCY NAME] allows service animals, visiting pets and approved resident-owned pets under the conditions below and consults the Department of Health's pet-facilitated therapy guidelines for any therapy animal program.

definitions.definition: Use of any lighted or heated tobacco, cannabis or similar product, and use of electronic smoking devices.
A posted outdoor area approved by the Administrator for smoking that is away from entrances, windows, air intakes and oxygen use.
A dog (or other animal permitted by law) individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability.
An animal brought in by a handler or program to provide comfort or therapy to residents, following DOH pet-facilitated therapy guidelines.
An animal owned by and cared for by a resident, approved in writing under this policy.

procedures: Disclosure: At pre-admission (ADM-01) the admissions staff explain the smoking policy, visitor policy and pet policy, and give the written rules with the admission agreement (RR-03). The resident or representative acknowledges receipt.
Signs: Maintenance staff post 'No Smoking' signs at entrances and in indoor common areas, and mark any designated outdoor smoking area. Signs are checked monthly.

Smoking assessment: At admission and reassessment (ADM-03), the RN assesses each resident who smokes for ability to smoke safely, including cognition, vision, dexterity, oxygen use and any history of burns or unsafe disposal. The results are recorded in the Health Service Plan (ADM-04).

Safe smoking: A resident who smokes goes to the designated area. If assessed as needing supervision or help, a staff member accompanies the resident. Lighters and matches are held by staff for residents who cannot use them safely. Ash is put in non-combustible containers that are emptied daily and kept away from buildings.
Oxygen: Residents on oxygen are not allowed to smoke or have a lighted item near the oxygen. Staff post oxygen signs on the unit door and remove the oxygen source before the resident goes to smoke.

Violations: Staff who see indoor smoking stop the activity, check for fire hazards, notify the nurse and Administrator and document the event. The Administrator speaks with the resident or visitor, reviews safety and revises the care plan. Repeated violations by a resident are addressed through care planning and, only as a last resort, the process in ADM-06.

Visiting hours: Visitors are welcome [VISITING HOURS]. The facility does not limit a resident's access to chosen visitors, including family, friends, clergy, the Ombudsman and representatives of agencies, except as stated here. Residents may also have visitors outside these hours with notice to staff.

Sign-in: Visitors sign in and out at the front desk with name, resident visited and time. The log is kept confidential and not shown to other visitors (RR-06). Staff may ask unfamiliar visitors who they are visiting and call the resident to confirm. Visitors for the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman, DOH surveyors and others with legal access are admitted at any time on showing identification.

Restricting a visit: Staff may limit or end a visit only to protect a resident from harm, for infection control, for disruptive behavior, or at the resident's request. The Administrator approves any ongoing restriction, informs the resident or representative and records the reason.

Privacy: Residents may meet visitors in their private units or in a private area. Staff do not discuss residents' information with visitors without the resident's or representative's permission (RR-06).

Pet approval: A resident who wishes to keep a pet submits a request to the Administrator. The Administrator and RN review the resident's ability to care for the animal, health and allergy effects on other residents and staff, the animal's behavior and the size and type of animal. Approval is in writing with conditions, and the resident acknowledges responsibility.

Pet conditions: The pet must have current rabies and other required vaccinations and licensing proof, must be healthy and non-aggressive, must be restrained in common areas and kept out of dining areas, food preparation areas and medication rooms. The resident arranges feeding, waste removal, grooming and veterinary care, and a backup caregiver if the resident cannot care for the pet. Staff are not required to provide the care unless the agreement says so.

Safeguards: The Administrator ensures the pet does not interfere in other residents' lives. This means no roaming unattended, no noise or odor complaints left unresolved, and no restriction of other residents' access to common areas. Residents with allergies, fear of animals or infection risk are protected. The Administrator may withdraw approval, with notice and a chance to rehome the animal, if conditions are not met.

Visiting and therapy animals: Therapy and visiting animals come only from an approved program or handler with vaccination proof, are supervised by the handler at all times, and visit only residents who agree. Visits are scheduled with the Activities Director and follow DOH pet-facilitated therapy guidelines.

Service animals: A service animal is allowed anywhere residents are allowed. Staff may ask only whether the animal is required because of a disability and what task it performs. The resident remains responsible for its care and control.

Complaints: Residents, families or staff can report concerns about smoking, visitors or animals to the Administrator. Residents may also contact the Department of Health or the Ombudsman without reprisal (RR-02). Complaints are logged and answered.
Review: The Administrator reviews this policy at least annually with the resident care policies (HLT-01, GOV-05) and documents the review.

responsibilities.duty: Sets and enforces smoking, visitor and pet rules; approves pets and visit restrictions; resolves complaints; documents annual review.
Assesses smoking safety and ability to care for pets, updates the Health Service Plan and reviews oxygen safety.
Maintains visitor log, greets visitors, calls residents to confirm visits and protects log privacy.
Supervise smoking as the care plan requires, enforce no-smoking rules, support visits and report problems.
Follow posted rules; residents with pets keep up care and vaccinations.
Post signs, keep the smoking area safe and clean.

documentation: Written smoking, visitor and pet policy given with the admission agreement and acknowledgment
Smoking safety assessment and Health Service Plan entries
Posted signs and designated smoking area record
Visitor log (kept confidential)
Visit restriction record with reason and approval
Pet approval agreement, vaccination records and any withdrawal notice
Therapy animal visit records
Complaint log entries and annual policy review record

policies.title: Security Policies and Procedures
policies.applies_to: ALR, CPCH and ALP; all residents, staff, visitors and vendors; building, grounds and all shifts
policies.purpose: To keep residents, staff and property safe by controlling entry, visitors and keys, maintaining night-time awareness and rounds, and responding to security events, while protecting residents' privacy, independence and right to leave and re-enter. This policy meets N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.7(a)3, policies and procedures for maintaining security.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.7(a)3, policies and procedures for maintaining security. [AGENCY NAME] maintains written security procedures covering entry control, visitor sign-in, key control, night-time rounds, staff awareness of exits and response to security events. These procedures are part of the Policy and Procedure Manual required by N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.7, are kept available in the facility to DOH representatives at all times, and are reviewed at least annually. In an ALR or CPCH, each resident unit has a lockable entrance door (N.J.A.C. 8:36-1.3). Residents control their own unit key or lock, subject to the emergency access rules below. At least one awake personal care assistant plus one additional employee are on the premises at all times, as the minimum staffing floor in STF-01 (more as resident acuity requires). Security measures protect safety without restricting residents' rights. They do not confine residents (SAF-04), and residents who are at risk of wandering are served under SAF-03 and HLT-06. In an ALP, the program coordinates security for resident units with the housing owner and the Administrator is responsible for the security of program space and operations.

definitions.definition: Procedures that regulate who enters the building, when and by which doors.
A key held by the facility that opens resident unit doors for emergencies and authorized entry; access is restricted and logged.
Scheduled walk-throughs by staff to check residents, doors, exits, alarms and common areas.
The door to a resident's unit that the resident can lock for privacy and security.
Unauthorized entry, theft, threat, violence, suspicious person, lost or stolen key, damage to security equipment or any event that endangers safety or property.

procedures: Building entry: Exterior doors are locked [EXTERIOR DOORS LOCKED TIME] to [EXTERIOR DOORS UNLOCKED TIME]. During those hours, visitors are admitted by staff only after identification. Exit doors always allow residents and staff to leave without a key from the inside as required by fire code. Exit alarms, if installed, are tested weekly and recorded.

Front desk: During the day the front desk is staffed by a named employee. On other shifts, the designated staff member watches the entrance by intercom, door chime or camera. Doors are not propped open. If cameras are used, they cover only entrances, exits and common areas, never bedrooms, bathrooms or private spaces, and their use is disclosed to residents.

Visitor sign-in: Visitors sign in and out with name, resident visited, time and, after hours, a photo ID check. Delivery people and vendors sign in and wear visitor badges. Contractors work only in authorized areas. Visitor logs are kept confidential under RR-06 and visiting rights are as in SAF-08.

Unknown persons: Staff politely ask unknown persons who they are visiting. If they cannot give a reason, staff escort them to the front desk and call the Administrator. A person who refuses to leave or is threatening is reported to police by calling 911.

Resident unit doors: Residents may lock their unit doors and keep their own key. Staff knock and announce themselves before entering and enter without permission only for emergencies, welfare checks or care in the Health Service Plan. Use of an emergency key is recorded in the Key Log with reason, time and staff name.

Key control: The Administrator keeps a list of master and emergency keys and who is issued each. Keys are kept in a locked box or key cabinet, signed for at shift start and return, and never given to visitors or contractors. Lost keys are reported to the Administrator at once and locks are changed or rekeyed if there is a risk of unauthorized entry. Medication area keys and controlled substance keys follow HLT-02.
Staff identification: Staff wear name badges with photo and job title. Visitors do not receive access to resident records, medication areas, offices or storage rooms.

Night-time rounds: On night shift, staff make documented rounds at least every [ROUNDS INTERVAL] to check residents as the Health Service Plans require, check exit doors, alarms, lighting and common areas, and record the time and findings on the Rounds Log. Residents with special needs get more frequent checks as ordered.

Staff awareness of exits: At orientation and each year, staff learn every exit, alarm and door-release method and the residents who are at risk of wandering. Staff check that exit alarms work at each shift start. An alarm sounding is answered immediately and the resident count is checked (SAF-03).

Resident movement: Residents may come and go according to their preferences and Health Service Plan. Staff ask residents who leave to tell staff for safety, especially at night, but do not stop capable residents from leaving. When a resident is not located or returns late, staff follow SAF-03.

Valuables and theft: Residents are encouraged to lock valuables in their units. Resident funds and property are protected under RR-04. Any theft or suspected theft of resident property or facility property is reported to the Administrator the same shift, documented and investigated, and police are notified as appropriate. Suspected theft by staff is also reviewed as possible exploitation (SAF-01). Theft of scheduled or controlled substances is reported to the NJ Department of Law and Public Safety, Enforcement Bureau of Professional Boards at (973) 648-4742 and to other authorities with jurisdiction (HLT-02).

Threats and violence: Staff who face a threatening person move residents to safety, avoid confrontation, call 911 and notify the Administrator. After the event, the Administrator checks on residents and staff, files an incident report under SAF-02 and reviews security measures.

Abuse and exploitation: Suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation of a resident is reported to the Department of Health Complaints Program at 1-800-792-9770 and, for a resident age 60 or older, to the State Long-Term Care Ombudsman at 1-877-582-6995, as stated in SAF-01.

Grounds, lighting and technology: Maintenance staff check exterior lighting, door locks, intercoms, cameras and alarms weekly, repair defects promptly and record the checks. Landscaping is kept trimmed to avoid hiding places.

Emergency coordination: Security procedures are coordinated with the emergency and fire plans so that locked doors never block evacuation. During emergencies, staff secure the building as directed by the senior person on duty (SAF-05, SAF-06).
Training: Staff receive training on this policy at hire and annually, including visitor control, key control, response to threats and handling of unauthorized entry (STF-03). Training is documented.

Review: The Administrator reviews security events, rounds logs and equipment checks at least quarterly with the Quality Improvement Committee (GOV-06). The Administrator reviews this policy at least annually as part of the manual review (GOV-05) and documents the changes.

responsibilities.duty: Sets security procedures, controls keys, investigates events, orders corrections and documents the annual review.
Controls entry and visitor sign-in and issues badges.
Makes rounds, checks doors and alarms, responds to security events and records findings.
Know exits and alarms, challenge unknown persons politely, protect keys and report events at once.
Maintain locks, lighting, alarms and cameras and record checks.
Are encouraged to lock their units, protect their keys and valuables and tell staff of security concerns.

documentation: Written security policy and annual review record
Visitor sign-in log (confidential)
Key list, key issue log and emergency key use log
Night-time Rounds Log and exit alarm test records
Security event and incident reports and police report numbers
Maintenance records for locks, lighting, cameras and alarms
Staff training records
QI committee minutes on security events

policies.title: Food Service, Dining and Therapeutic Diets
policies.applies_to: ALR, CPCH, ALP (congregate dining requirements apply to the ALR; ALP and CPCH apply the sections that match the services they provide)
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident receives nutritionally adequate, safely prepared, appetizing meals in a dining setting that respects personal preference, and that therapeutic diets are ordered, planned, served and monitored correctly.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides dining services as part of the personal care and services it must be capable of providing under N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.1. Dining services are congregate: residents are offered meals in a common dining area, and a resident who cannot or chooses not to attend is offered tray service in the unit. The nutrients and calories offered to each resident follow the Dietary Reference Intake tables of the Food and Nutrition Board (National Academies), adjusted for the resident's age, sex, weight, physical activity and therapeutic needs, as required by N.J.A.C. 8:36-10.5(c)6. The facility designates a food services coordinator and uses a dietitian who meets the qualifications in the dining services subchapter of N.J.A.C. 8:36. Therapeutic diets are served only on a physician's order and are recorded in the resident's service plan. Residents' food preferences, cultural and religious practices, and swallowing and chewing needs are honored whenever safe.

definitions.definition: The nutrient and energy reference tables published by the Food and Nutrition Board of the National Academies, used by the facility as the standard for resident nutrition planning.
A diet ordered by a physician to treat a medical condition, such as diabetic, low-sodium, renal, texture-modified or thickened-liquid diets.
The employee designated by the Administrator to manage menu planning, food purchasing, preparation, service and sanitation.
Meals served to residents together in a shared dining room.
A registered dietitian or other person meeting the dietitian qualifications in the dining services subchapter of N.J.A.C. 8:36, who reviews menus and advises on therapeutic diets.

procedures: The Administrator designates in writing a food services coordinator and records the designation in the organizational chart (GOV-01). The coordinator's training and any food safety certification are filed in the personnel record (STF-05).

The Administrator retains a dietitian, as an employee or consultant, who meets the qualifications in the dining services subchapter. The dietitian's credentials are kept on file and verified before the first consultation.

The dietitian and food services coordinator write cycle menus that meet the Dietary Reference Intake tables as required by N.J.A.C. 8:36-10.5(c)6. The dietitian reviews and signs the menus before use and at least annually, and again whenever a major menu change is made.
Menus are posted where residents can see them. Substitutions are written on the posted menu or the daily menu record and must be of comparable nutritional value.

At admission and at each reassessment (ADM-03), the RN or designee records food allergies, intolerances, preferences, cultural or religious restrictions, chewing and swallowing ability, weight, and any diet order. These are entered in the service plan (ADM-04).

A therapeutic diet starts only on a written or verified telephone order from the resident's physician or other authorized prescriber. The nurse transcribes the order to the service plan and gives the food services coordinator the diet order within the same shift.

The food services coordinator keeps a current diet roster in the kitchen. The roster lists each resident's diet, texture, liquid consistency, allergies and tray or dining-room status. The nurse updates the roster the same day a diet order changes.

Dietitian review of each resident on a therapeutic diet occurs at admission and at least with each reassessment. The dietitian's recommendations are sent to the RN, who relays them to the prescriber and updates the service plan.
The facility serves meals at set times posted for residents [MEAL SERVICE HOURS]. Snacks and fluids are available between meals. A resident who misses a meal is offered a substitute meal.

Dining room staff are trained in each resident's diet, assistance with eating, aspiration precautions and food allergy response. Staff who assist with feeding are observed by the nurse as part of competency checks (STF-03).

Staff weigh residents on admission and at least monthly [WEIGHT SCHEDULE]. Unplanned weight change, poor intake or refusal of meals over [NUMBER] consecutive meals is reported to the RN the same day and handled under HLT-05.

Food is purchased, stored, prepared, held and served in accordance with applicable state and local food safety requirements. The food services coordinator keeps refrigerator and freezer temperature logs, dish-machine logs and cleaning schedules, and reviews them weekly.
Food workers with vomiting, diarrhea, fever or infected wounds are not allowed to handle food and are managed under STF-04 and SAF-07.
Residents may refuse a diet. The nurse documents the refusal, explains the risk, notifies the physician, and discusses a managed risk agreement under ADM-04 where appropriate.

The food services coordinator reports resident and family dining concerns to the Administrator and brings them to the resident council and the QI committee (GOV-06). Dining satisfaction and weight trends are reviewed at least quarterly.
The food services coordinator keeps the emergency menu and a supply of food and water for the period required by the facility emergency plan (SAF-05).

responsibilities.duty: Designates the food services coordinator, secures dietitian services, and makes sure meals and staff are adequate.
Plans and produces menus, maintains the diet roster and sanitation logs, supervises dietary staff and ensures safe food handling.
Reviews menus against the Dietary Reference Intakes, evaluates residents on therapeutic diets and recommends changes.
Records diet needs in the service plan, obtains and transcribes physician orders, and responds to weight loss and swallowing concerns.

responsibilities.role: Personal care assistants and dining staff
responsibilities.duty: Serve meals as ordered, assist residents to eat, record intake, and report changes to the nurse.
Orders therapeutic diets and reviews them as needed.

documentation: Dated cycle menus with dietitian signature
Diet orders and the service plan diet entry
Daily diet roster
Dietitian consultation and review notes
Weight records
Temperature, cleaning and food-safety logs
Meal refusal and managed risk documentation
Food services coordinator designation and credential records

policies.title: Activities, Social Programming and Social Isolation Prevention
policies.applies_to: ALR, CPCH, ALP
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident has meaningful, voluntary activities that match his or her interests and abilities, and to prevent social isolation.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] is capable of providing activities, recreation and social work services, as required by N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.1(b), and provides resident activities in accordance with N.J.A.C. 8:36-12.1. The facility offers a varied calendar of group and individual activities matched to resident interests, abilities, culture and language, including residents with dementia and residents who stay in their units. Participation is always voluntary. The facility also follows the social isolation prevention requirements of N.J.A.C. 8:36 in effect at the time, and the Administrator confirms the current text with the Department of Health each year when this policy is reviewed. The facility records participation and uses it to identify residents who are becoming isolated.

definitions.definition: The scheduled and unscheduled social, recreational, physical, spiritual, creative, educational and community activities offered by the facility.
A pattern of little or no social contact or engagement that places a resident at risk of decline, depression or loneliness.
A structured interview of the resident and family about past and present interests, routines, faith, language and abilities.
The employee designated by the Administrator to plan, lead and document the activity program.

procedures: The Administrator designates an activities coordinator and records the designation in the organizational chart (GOV-01). The coordinator completes orientation and annual training on assisted living activities, dementia engagement and social isolation (STF-03).

At admission, the activities coordinator or social worker completes an activity preference assessment with the resident and, with permission, family. The results are entered in the service plan (ADM-04) within the time period set for the initial service plan.

The activities coordinator develops a monthly calendar that includes physical, social, cognitive, creative, spiritual and community activities. At least [NUMBER] activities are offered each day, including some in the evening and on weekends.
The calendar is posted in common areas, given to each resident, and placed in each unit. Large print and translated or interpreted versions are provided on request (RR-07).

Activities are offered to residents of all functional levels. For residents with dementia, the coordinator provides small-group, sensory, reminiscence and structured programs matched to cognitive ability, as set out in HLT-06.

Residents who do not leave their units, are in bed, or decline group programs are offered one-to-one visits at least [FREQUENCY] and given materials, music, reading or calls matched to their interests.
Residents may propose activities and trips. The coordinator reviews requests with the resident council each month and documents the response.
Staff help residents who need assistance to attend and return from activities. Needs for assistive devices, hearing aids and wheelchairs are checked before each event.
Participation in each activity is recorded on an attendance record by the person leading it, including individual and in-room visits and the resident's response.

The activities coordinator reviews the attendance records at least monthly and lists any resident who rarely or never participates, who has stopped participating, or who shows signs of withdrawal. The coordinator refers each such resident to the social worker and nurse within 3 business days.

The social worker or designee meets with the referred resident, identifies barriers such as pain, mobility, hearing, vision, mood, language, culture or lack of interest, and updates the service plan with specific interventions (HLT-11, ADM-04).
Resident refusal is respected and documented without penalty. A resident is never required to take part in an activity as a condition of residency.
Outings follow DL-04. Activities involving food follow the resident's diet order (DL-01). Residents at risk of elopement are supervised as set out in SAF-03.
The facility encourages visits, volunteers, faith groups, community programs and family events, consistent with SAF-08.
Activities supplies and space are kept clean, safe and in good repair. Equipment that is broken is removed from use and reported on the work-order log (DL-03).
The Administrator reports activity participation, isolation referrals and resident feedback to the QI committee at least quarterly (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Provides staff, space and budget, designates the activities coordinator and confirms the current regulatory text yearly.
Assesses preferences, plans and leads activities, records participation and refers isolated residents.
Follows up on isolation referrals, counsels residents and families and updates the service plan.
Identifies health barriers to participation and adjusts the service plan.
Assist residents to attend activities and report withdrawal or loss of interest.

documentation: Activity preference assessments
Monthly calendars
Daily attendance and individual-visit records
Monthly isolation review and referrals
Service plan interventions
Resident council minutes
QI committee reports

policies.title: Housekeeping, Laundry, Pest Control and Maintenance
policies.applies_to: ALR, CPCH, ALP
policies.purpose: To keep the residence clean, sanitary, safe, comfortable and in good repair, and to protect residents and staff from infection, pests and hazardous waste.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains the building, grounds and equipment in accordance with N.J.A.C. 8:36-17, which covers housekeeping, laundry, pest control, resident environment, waste removal, sanitation, and heating and air conditioning. The facility keeps a written housekeeping work plan and uses trained staff to carry it out. Regulated medical waste and sharps are handled according to OSHA's bloodborne pathogens standard, 29 CFR 1910.1030, and state and local law. All maintenance requests are logged on a work-order log and tracked until complete.

definitions.definition: A written schedule listing the areas, tasks, frequency, products, and responsible staff for cleaning the residence.
Waste containing blood or other potentially infectious material, including sharps, handled and disposed of as required by law.
Needles, lancets, syringes and other items that can puncture skin.
The record of each maintenance or repair request, the date, the person responsible, the action and the completion date.
A pest control approach using inspection, prevention and the least hazardous effective treatment.

procedures: The Administrator designates a housekeeping and laundry supervisor and a maintenance lead in writing and records them in the organizational chart (GOV-01).

The housekeeping supervisor writes a housekeeping work plan covering resident units, common areas, dining and kitchen areas, bathrooms and entrances. The plan lists tasks, frequency, products and responsible staff. The Administrator approves it, and it is reviewed at least annually.

Housekeeping staff are trained before working alone on cleaning methods, product use and safety data sheets, hand hygiene, personal protective equipment, handling of bodily fluids, and the bloodborne pathogens standard (29 CFR 1910.1030). Training is recorded in the personnel record (STF-03, STF-05).

Resident units are cleaned on the schedule in the work plan and any time a resident asks for cleaning or a spill or soiling occurs. Housekeeping staff respect the resident's privacy and belongings (RR-06).

Soiled linens and clothing are handled with gloves, bagged where they are used, and moved to the laundry without shaking. Soiled items are kept separate from clean items in processing, storage and transport. Residents' personal clothing is labeled and washed separately from facility linens.
The facility keeps adequate clean linen on hand. Clean linen is stored covered, away from soiled items and from chemicals.

The facility contracts with a licensed pest control company, or has a trained employee do the work, to carry out an integrated pest management program. Treatments are scheduled with notice to residents. Records show the dates, areas treated and products used. Sightings of pests are reported at once to the maintenance lead, who arranges treatment within [TIME FRAME].
Trash and waste are collected from units and common areas at least daily, kept in covered containers and removed from the building on a regular schedule to a secured outdoor area that is kept clean.

Regulated medical waste and sharps are placed in puncture-resistant, labeled containers at the point of use and are never recapped, bent or broken. Full containers are sealed, stored in a locked area, and collected by a licensed medical waste hauler. The facility keeps hauler contracts and manifests. Resident needle and syringe disposal follows SAF-07.
Any staff member who has an exposure incident reports it to the nurse at once and follows the exposure control plan under SAF-07 and STF-04.
Any staff member or resident may report a maintenance concern by telling any employee or by completing a work-order request. The receiving employee enters it on the work-order log the same day.

The maintenance lead reviews the work-order log each business day. Hazardous conditions such as no heat, no cooling, no hot water, leaks, electrical hazards, broken locks, blocked exits or loose handrails are corrected immediately or the area is blocked off and residents are protected, and the Administrator is told at once.

The maintenance lead inspects heating and air conditioning systems, water temperature, lighting, floors, handrails, call systems and grounds on a written preventive maintenance schedule. Contractors serve boilers, HVAC, elevators, fire protection and generators as required (SAF-06, SAF-05). Records are kept on site.
Heating and cooling are maintained so that resident units and common areas stay at a comfortable temperature. Residents may adjust the temperature in their units within safe limits.
Chemicals are stored in locked or restricted areas away from food and medications. Safety data sheets are available to staff for every product.
The Administrator reviews the work-order log, completed inspections and any housekeeping complaints monthly and reports trends to the QI committee (GOV-06). Failures are corrected and documented.

responsibilities.duty: Approves the work plan, funds maintenance and pest control, and reviews logs monthly.
Writes and supervises the work plan, trains staff and inspects cleaning results.
Manages the work-order log, preventive maintenance, pest control and contractors.
Carry out the work plan, follow infection control and bloodborne pathogens practices and report hazards.
Oversees sharps and medical waste practice and exposure incidents with the infection preventionist.
Report spills, hazards, pests and needed repairs the same day.

documentation: Written housekeeping work plan
Housekeeping training records
Cleaning logs and inspection checklists
Work-order log
Pest control contract, treatment and service reports
Medical waste hauler contract and manifests
Preventive maintenance and contractor service records
Safety data sheets

policies.title: Resident Transportation
policies.applies_to: ALR, CPCH, ALP
policies.purpose: To make sure residents have safe, accessible transportation to medical appointments, community activities and other needs, and that residents know in advance what transportation is included and what costs extra.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides or coordinates transportation as part of the personal care and services it must provide or coordinate under N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.1. Transportation is provided without discrimination and with reasonable accommodation for residents with disabilities, consistent with the Americans with Disabilities Act (42 USC 12101). The admission agreement states which transportation is included in the base rate and which is available at extra cost (RR-03). The facility has a written plan for emergency transport. Staff who drive residents hold a valid license, drive insured vehicles and receive training, and wheelchairs are properly secured.

definitions.definition: Planned trips arranged in advance, such as medical appointments, shopping or outings.
Transport of a resident by ambulance or emergency medical services in an urgent or life-threatening situation.
Use of a vehicle's tie-down and occupant restraint system to fix a wheelchair and its occupant for travel.
A staff member or other designated person who accompanies a resident on a trip.

procedures: The Administrator designates a transportation coordinator and records the designation in the organizational chart (GOV-01).

Before admission, the admission staff member explains transportation in writing: which trips are included in the base rate, the days and times of the facility vehicle, the limits on distance or number of trips, and the fees for trips not included. The same terms are written in the admission agreement (RR-03). Any change in fees is given in writing according to RR-03.

Residents or their representatives ask for scheduled rides with the transportation coordinator at least [NOTICE PERIOD] before the trip. The coordinator logs the request, the date, the destination, the mobility needs and the escort needs, and confirms the ride with the resident.

The coordinator keeps the schedule of trips and tells the nurse of any appointment that requires medication, paperwork, medical records or orders to go with the resident. The nurse prepares an information sheet containing current medications, diagnoses, allergies, advance directive status (RR-05) and emergency contact for the resident to take.

The nurse decides whether a resident needs an escort based on cognition, safety, behavior and care needs. If an escort is required, the coordinator assigns one before the trip. Residents at risk of elopement are never transported unaccompanied (SAF-03).

Staff who drive residents must be at least 21 [MINIMUM DRIVER AGE], hold a valid New Jersey driver's license for the class of vehicle, and have a satisfactory driving record check before they drive. Records are kept in the personnel record (STF-05).

Drivers are trained before first use in safe driving, vehicle operation, lift operation, wheelchair securement, passenger assistance, sensitivity to persons with disabilities, emergency procedures and infection control. Training is documented and repeated annually (STF-03).

Facility vehicles are insured under a policy that covers passengers and are registered, inspected and maintained under a written schedule. The maintenance lead checks tires, lights, brakes, lifts, tie-downs and seat belts before each day of use, and records the check on a vehicle log. A vehicle with a safety defect is taken out of service.

Wheelchairs are secured by a four-point tie-down and the occupant uses a lap and shoulder belt. Residents are transferred to a vehicle seat when appropriate and safe. Drivers do not transport residents on stretchers unless the vehicle is designed for it.
Staff provide assistance getting in and out of the vehicle at both ends of the trip, and do not leave residents who need supervision alone in or near a vehicle.

Accessible vehicles or arrangements with an accessible transport provider are used for residents who use wheelchairs or other mobility devices. The facility does not refuse a trip solely because of disability and makes reasonable modifications. If the facility cannot provide the ride, the coordinator helps the resident find another accessible option.

The facility's emergency transport plan requires staff to call 911 for any life-threatening condition, then notify the nurse, the physician and the representative (HLT-05). The nurse sends the resident with the current medication list, face sheet and advance directive information. A staff member follows or calls the hospital to confirm arrival.

If a vehicle breaks down, there is an accident or a resident becomes ill during a trip, the driver stops safely, calls 911 if needed, contacts the Administrator or designee, and follows SAF-02 for incident reporting. Residents are checked for injury and assisted to alternate transport.

Residents using community transit, family or medical transport providers are offered help with scheduling and the information sheet. The facility keeps a list of local accessible transport providers [LOCAL TRANSPORT RESOURCES] and, for NJ FamilyCare members, helps arrange covered non-emergency medical transportation through the member's managed care plan (ADM-07).
The Administrator reviews the transportation log, vehicle records, complaints and incidents at least quarterly and reports to the QI committee (GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures insurance, vehicles, drivers and funding, and approves transportation terms in the admission agreement.
Schedules trips, assigns drivers and escorts, keeps logs and arranges alternative transport.
Hold a valid license, complete training, inspect vehicles, secure passengers and report incidents.
Determines escort needs and prepares medical information for trips and emergency transfers.
Explain included and extra-cost transportation before the agreement is signed.

documentation: Transportation terms in the admission agreement
Trip request and schedule log
Driver license, driving record and training records
Vehicle insurance, registration, inspection and maintenance logs
Daily vehicle safety check log
Resident information sheets for trips
Incident reports
Quarterly transportation review

policies.title: Staffing Levels, Supervision and Wage Compliance
policies.applies_to: ALR, CPCH, ALP
policies.purpose: To make sure enough qualified staff are on duty at all times to meet resident needs, that nursing is available and supervision is clear, and that all employees are paid in accordance with state and federal wage law.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps, at all times on the premises, at least one awake personal care assistant (PCA) and at least one additional employee, as required by N.J.A.C. 8:36-9.3. If the facility has more than one free-standing building with residents, at least one PCA is on duty in each building, and both PCAs must be awake. These levels are minimums only. The facility sets and adjusts staffing so that it is sufficient in number and training for the assessed acuity of residents. At least one registered professional nurse is available at all times and each resident receives an RN assessment and care plan, as required by N.J.A.C. 8:36-8.2. The facility pays every employee at least the New Jersey minimum wage, which is $15.92 per hour effective January 1, 2026 under N.J.A.C. 12:56-3.1, and complies with federal wage and hour rules for home care workers under 29 CFR 552.

definitions.definition: A facility employee who is certified as a PCA, or as a certified nurse aide, under N.J.A.C. 8:36-9.1.
Alert, on duty and available to residents; not sleeping.
A separate building in which residents live, where a separate PCA must be present.
The level of care needs of the residents, based on assessments, such as ADL dependence, cognition, behavior and nursing needs.
The least number of staff permitted by regulation. Safe staffing may require more.
A registered professional nurse is on duty or on call, available as defined in the facility's written RN coverage plan, which the Administrator has confirmed with the Department of Health.

procedures: The Administrator, with the director of nursing or RN, writes a staffing plan that states, for each shift and each building, the number and type of staff. The plan can never be lower than the minimum in N.J.A.C. 8:36-9.3: one awake PCA and one additional employee on the premises at all times, and, where residents live in more than one free-standing building, at least one awake PCA in each building.

The Administrator confirms with the Department of Health what RN availability means for on-site and on-call coverage and response time under N.J.A.C. 8:36-8.2. The agreed standard is written into the RN coverage plan [RN COVERAGE AND RESPONSE STANDARD], and every employee is told how to reach the RN at all hours.

Each day the Administrator posts a nurse and PCA roster for each shift showing names, titles, certification status and the on-call RN with telephone number. The roster is kept for review by the Department of Health.

At least monthly, and whenever there is an admission, a discharge or a change in a resident's condition, the RN totals the acuity of residents from the assessments (ADM-03) and service plans (ADM-04), including ADL dependence, dementia, behaviors, two-person transfers, nursing-home-level residents (ADM-02), falls risk and medication needs.

The Administrator and RN compare the acuity summary with the schedule. If acuity requires more staff than the minimum, such as more PCAs, awake overnight staff, a medication aide or an RN on site, the Administrator adds staff for the affected shifts and records the change and the reason in the staffing plan.
The facility does not admit or retain a resident whose needs exceed what the staffing plan can safely meet (ADM-01, ADM-05).

The scheduler may not count in the minimum staffing any employee who is not on the premises, who is a trainee not yet certified, who is sleeping, or who is also assigned to another building. Staff in orientation are supervised and are counted only when they are certified and have completed required training (STF-03).

The scheduler makes sure that the PCA counted for each building is certified and verified under STF-02, and that medication administration is done only by licensed nurses or certified medication aides (HLT-03).

If an employee calls out or leaves early, the shift supervisor calls the on-call list, uses overtime or agency staff who have completed STF-02 screening, and notifies the Administrator. The facility never goes below the minimum on the premises. If a replacement is not found, the Administrator or designee who is qualified comes in, and the shortfall is recorded.

A clear supervisor is named on every shift. The RN supervises PCAs and medication aides for care duties, and the Administrator or designee supervises other staff. Delegation follows HLT-04 and the Nurse Practice Act.
The Administrator is on site or reachable at all times, or has a qualified designee in charge when absent (STF-07).

At least once each quarter the Administrator reviews staffing against call-light or response times, incidents, falls, complaints and resident or family concerns, and reports to the QI committee (GOV-06). Where there is a pattern of delayed care, staffing is raised.

All employees are paid at least the New Jersey minimum wage of $15.92 per hour effective January 1, 2026. The Administrator or payroll manager checks every pay rate, including those of trainees, before the effective date. When the New Jersey Department of Labor and Workforce Development publishes the CPI-adjusted 2027 rate, expected about September 30, 2026, payroll updates all rates before it takes effect.

The facility is a third-party employer of home care workers and follows the federal wage and hour rules at 29 CFR 552. It does not rely on the companionship or live-in exemptions for overtime without written advice from counsel. Non-exempt employees are paid overtime at one and one-half times the regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek, and time worked is recorded accurately by time clock or system.

The payroll manager audits timekeeping and pay at least quarterly, including meal breaks, on-call time, mandatory training time and overtime, and corrects underpayments with back pay promptly. Records of hours and wages are kept as required by the New Jersey Department of Labor and Workforce Development and federal law.
The Administrator keeps the staffing plan, rosters and acuity reviews for review at survey and posts the required wage and labor notices where employees can see them.

responsibilities.duty: Funds staffing at the level needed for resident acuity, and reviews staffing reports.
Writes and approves the staffing plan, assures minimums are never missed, confirms RN availability and oversees wage compliance.
Completes acuity reviews, recommends staffing changes and supervises nursing care.
Builds rosters, fills vacancies and verifies certification of staff counted in the minimum.
Pays at least the minimum wage and overtime, keeps time and pay records and updates rates for new minimum wage.
Remain awake and on duty at assigned building and report staffing problems at once.

documentation: Written staffing plan with minimums and acuity adjustments
Daily and weekly rosters and time records
RN coverage plan and on-call schedule
Monthly acuity review
Call-out and replacement records
Quarterly staffing review and QI minutes
Payroll records, pay rate schedule and wage audits
Posted labor notices

policies.title: Background Checks, Registries and Staff Certification Verification
policies.applies_to: ALR, CPCH, ALP
policies.purpose: To make sure that no person works with residents until criminal history and registry screening are complete and required certifications are verified, and that certifications and checks stay current.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] screens every person who will provide care or work in the residence before that person is scheduled. Personal care assistant (PCA) certification requires a criminal history record background check under N.J.A.C. 8:43I. The certification is valid for 2 years, and renewal requires an updated check, as required by N.J.A.C. 8:36-9.1 and N.J.S.A. 26:2H-83 et seq. (follow-up federal criminal history check at least every two years). Assisted living administrators also complete a background check for certification and recertification under N.J.A.C. 8:36-3.2 and N.J.A.C. 8:43I. The facility checks the PCA abuse registry and the medication aide abuse registry before hire, verifies certification, and keeps proof in the personnel file. No one is scheduled before screening is complete.

definitions.definition: The state and federal fingerprint-based check of criminal records required for certification or recertification under N.J.A.C. 8:43I.

definitions.term: Certified personal care assistant or nurse aide
definitions.definition: A person who has completed a DOH-approved course and exam or competency evaluation and holds current certification (N.J.A.C. 8:36-9.1).
A person who has completed a DOH-approved medication administration course and passed a DOH-approved exam (N.J.A.C. 8:36-9.2).
The Department of Health registries of PCAs and medication aides with findings of abuse, neglect, misappropriation (and, for medication aides, negligence or incompetence).
The process available under N.J.A.C. 8:43I for a person with a disqualifying conviction to show rehabilitation.
All checks required by this policy are back, reviewed and recorded as clear, and certification is verified.

procedures: Before an offer is made, the Administrator or human resources designee tells the candidate in writing that employment depends on the completed background check, registry checks, certification verification and health screening (STF-04).

For PCA positions, the designee checks that the candidate holds a current PCA or certified nurse aide certification from the Department of Health, using the Department's verification process. Verification is printed or screen-captured, dated and signed by the person who checked it.

For a candidate in a certification process, the facility confirms the candidate's status and does not count the candidate as a PCA in the staffing minimum (STF-01) or leave the candidate unsupervised with residents until certified and screened.

The criminal history record background check required by N.J.A.C. 8:43I is started for every PCA, nurse aide and assisted living administrator candidate or recertification, following the Department's current instructions for fingerprinting and submission. The designee records the date submitted and the date the result is received.

The designee checks the Department of Health PCA abuse registry and the medication aide abuse registry before hire for every candidate who will give care, and records the date, the registry and the finding. A candidate with a registry finding is not hired.

For certified medication aides, the designee verifies current certification and, at hire and at each renewal, that the aide has finished the required continuing education: 10 hours per 2-year period, 5 on fundamentals of medication administration and 5 on drug use relevant to the elderly (N.J.A.C. 8:36-9.2).

The designee reviews each result with the Administrator. A disqualifying conviction or unresolved result means the person is not scheduled. If the candidate pursues a determination of rehabilitation under N.J.A.C. 8:43I, the facility does not allow the person to work with residents until the Department's determination is received and the Administrator has approved employment in writing.

No person is placed on a schedule, counted in staffing, or allowed unsupervised access to residents or their records until screening is complete and the Administrator or designee has signed the screening completion checklist.

Other staff (such as dietary, housekeeping, maintenance, activities and agency or contract staff) who are not covered by N.J.A.C. 8:43I are screened according to the facility's hiring policy, including a reference check and registry check where applicable (STF-03). Agency or contract staff must be verified to the same standard before the first shift, and the contract requires the agency to supply proof.

The designee keeps a certification and screening tracker listing each employee's certification type, number, issue and expiry dates, last background check date, registry check dates and continuing education. The tracker is reviewed monthly.

The designee flags every PCA and medication aide at least 120 days before certification expires. The employee must submit recertification and the updated criminal history check at least 60 days before expiry. The Administrator is told of any employee at risk of lapsing.

If a certification or required check lapses, the Administrator removes the employee from the schedule at the end of the shift in which the lapse is found. The employee works only in non-care duties, if at all, until the certification is renewed and verified. The Administrator records the lapse and the action.

For the Administrator, the facility keeps proof of the current 3-year assisted living administrator certification or nursing home administrator license, proof of at least 30 hours of assisted living continuing education earned in the certificate period, and proof of the background check at renewal (N.J.A.C. 8:36-3.2, STF-07). The governing body checks this record at least annually.

Employees must report to the Administrator within [NUMBER] days any arrest, charge or conviction, and any notice from the Department of Health about their certification, a registry entry or a hearing. Failure to report is grounds for discipline.

If a staff member is accused of abuse, neglect or misappropriation, the facility reports it as required by SAF-01 and SAF-02 and removes the person from resident contact while the matter is reviewed. The Department of Health may review and, for a finding, list a PCA on the abuse registry or a medication aide on the medication aide registry after notice and a hearing opportunity. The Administrator cooperates and records the result.

Original reports of background checks and registry results are kept in a restricted file apart from the general personnel file, are available to the Department of Health at survey, and are kept in line with STF-05 and REC-01. Results are not shared except as the law allows (RR-06).

responsibilities.duty: Makes the final decision on hiring, approves screening completion and handles disqualifying results and lapses.
Starts checks, checks registries, verifies certifications, maintains the tracker and issues renewal alerts.
Schedules only employees marked as screening complete on the tracker.
Provide accurate information, renew certification on time and report arrests or notices.
Reviews annual verification of administrator certification and screening compliance.

documentation: Screening completion checklist signed by the Administrator
Certification verification printouts
Criminal history background check submission and result records (restricted file)
PCA and medication aide registry check records
Continuing education records for medication aides and the administrator
Certification and screening tracker
Rehabilitation determination records, if any
Lapse and corrective action notes
Agency or contract staff verification records

policies.title: Hiring, Orientation and Ongoing Training
policies.applies_to: All employees and contract staff of [AGENCY NAME], with emphasis on personal care assistants (PCAs), certified medication aides (CMAs) and all other direct caregivers
policies.purpose: To make sure every person who gives direct care at [AGENCY NAME] holds the required New Jersey credentials, is oriented before or on the date of employment, and receives ongoing in-service education, and to keep proof of all of it in the personnel file.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] hires only people who meet the credential requirements for the position. A PCA must be a facility employee who has either (a) completed a DOH-approved nurse aide course (N.J.A.C. 8:39-43) and passed the NJ Nurse Aide Certification Exam, or (b) completed a DOH-approved PCA course and competency evaluation leading to PCA certification (N.J.A.C. 8:36-9.1). PCA certification requires the criminal history background check under N.J.A.C. 8:43I, is valid for 2 years, and is renewed only with an updated check. A certified medication aide must complete a DOH-approved medication administration course and pass a DOH-approved exam (N.J.A.C. 8:36-9.2). Each PCA and direct caregiver receives orientation before or on the date of employment and ongoing in-service on assisted living concepts (N.J.A.C. 8:36-9.1). In-service also covers emergency plans, infection control, resident rights, abuse and neglect, and dementia care. The Administrator confirms the full list of required topics against the current N.J.A.C. 8:36 at each annual manual review (see GOV-05). If [AGENCY NAME] advertises or holds itself out as having an Alzheimer's disease or dementia program, all licensed and unlicensed staff who give direct care to residents with Alzheimer's or dementia complete the mandatory training required by N.J.S.A. 26:2M-7.2 (N.J.A.C. 8:36-19.3). Orientation and in-service are documented in the personnel file (see STF-05). Staff with occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials receive bloodborne pathogen training under 29 CFR 1910.1030.

definitions.definition: A facility employee who holds PCA certification, or who completed a DOH-approved nurse aide course and passed the NJ Nurse Aide Certification Exam, as described in N.J.A.C. 8:36-9.1.
An employee who completed a DOH-approved medication administration course, passed a DOH-approved exam, and keeps the certification current under N.J.A.C. 8:36-9.2.
Training given before or on the date of employment, before the employee works unsupervised with residents.
Ongoing training given after orientation, planned and documented by the Administrator.
Any employee or contract worker who provides hands-on care or assistance to residents.

procedures: Before making an offer for a PCA, CMA, nursing or other direct care position, the Administrator or designee reviews the job description and the credentials required for the role.
The hiring manager collects a signed application with work history, education and references, and copies of all certificates and licenses presented.

For PCA applicants, the hiring manager verifies the nurse aide or PCA certification with the DOH certification and registry records and keeps a dated copy of the verification in the personnel file (see STF-02).

For CMA applicants, the hiring manager verifies the CMA certification and expiration date and that no abuse registry finding exists. The medication aide's biennial renewal date is entered on the credential tracking log.
A PCA applicant who has not yet been certified is not scheduled as a PCA and is not counted toward staffing minimums (see STF-01) until certification is verified.
Background checks and registry checks required by STF-02 are completed before the employee gives unsupervised resident care.
The employee's health clearance required by STF-04 is on file before the first resident contact.

On or before the first day of work, the Administrator or a designated trainer delivers written and hands-on orientation to each PCA and direct caregiver. Orientation covers assisted living concepts, resident rights (RR-01), abuse, neglect and exploitation reporting (SAF-01), incident reporting (SAF-02), emergency and fire procedures (SAF-05, SAF-06), infection control and bloodborne pathogens (SAF-07), confidentiality (RR-06), security (SAF-09), elopement response (SAF-03), the job description, and the services [AGENCY NAME] can and cannot provide (GOV-02, ADM-05).

New direct care staff work alongside an experienced, qualified employee for their first scheduled shifts until the trainer signs off that the employee is competent in the tasks assigned. The sign-off is dated and placed in the file.

Before an employee works with residents who have dementia, the employee completes the dementia training described in HLT-06. If [AGENCY NAME] advertises a dementia program, all direct care staff complete the N.J.S.A. 26:2M-7.2 training. The Administrator requests the current mandatory training program in writing from the Division of Health Facility Survey and Field Operations (PO Box 367, Trenton, NJ 08625-0358).
Each orientation is recorded on an orientation checklist that lists topics, date, trainer name and employee signature, and the checklist is filed in the personnel file.

The Administrator prepares an annual in-service calendar. The calendar covers the topics in procedure 8, assisted living concepts, medication safety, fall prevention, skin integrity, change of condition and dementia care. [AGENCY NAME] sets a minimum of 12 hours of documented in-service per year for direct care staff. This is an agency standard and does not replace any higher number DOH may set.
Each in-service session is documented with date, topic, presenter, length and an attendance sheet with signatures. A copy of the individual's attendance is placed in each attendee's personnel file.
Employees who miss a session complete a make-up session within 30 days. The Administrator reviews the attendance tracking log monthly.

CMAs are tracked for their 2-year renewal and the 10 hours of continuing education per period (5 hours on fundamentals of medication administration and 5 on drug use relevant to the elderly). The Administrator checks the log 90 days before each expiration date. A CMA whose certification lapses stops administering medication immediately (see HLT-03).

PCAs are tracked for their 2-year certification expiration. [AGENCY NAME] requires renewal paperwork and the updated criminal history check to be started at least 90 days before expiration, and a PCA whose certification lapses is removed from PCA duties until renewal is verified.
Bloodborne pathogen training under 29 CFR 1910.1030 is given at hire, before any exposure risk, and at least annually afterwards.
Competency is checked at least annually through direct observation of resident care tasks by the RN or Administrator. Results are documented and used in the job performance evaluation.
The Administrator reviews the training program annually as part of the manual review and updates it for regulatory changes, survey findings and quality improvement findings (GOV-05, GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Ensures credential verification, orientation, in-service, dementia training and tracking are completed and documented; reviews the training program annually.
Delivers clinical training, observes competency and signs off on direct care skills.
Collects and verifies credentials, maintains tracking logs and files records in the personnel file.
Complete orientation and in-service, keep their credentials current and report any change in certification status immediately.

documentation: Credential verification copies with date and verifier initials
Orientation checklist signed by employee and trainer
Competency sign-off forms
In-service calendar, attendance sheets and individual training records
Dementia training records
Credential and certification expiration tracking log
Annual competency evaluation

policies.title: Employee Health, Physical Examinations, Immunizations and Tuberculosis Screening
policies.applies_to: All employees and all individuals who provide direct resident care services in the facility through contractual arrangements or written agreement
policies.purpose: To protect residents and staff from communicable disease by requiring physical examinations, immunizations and tuberculin testing on employment and at set intervals afterward, and to meet the policy requirement of N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.7(a)7.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.7(a)7, which requires policies and procedures, including content and frequency, for physical examinations, immunizations and tuberculin testing on employment and afterward for employees and for individuals providing direct resident care services in the facility through contractual arrangements or written agreement. No employee or contract caregiver has resident contact until a pre-employment physical examination and a baseline tuberculosis screening are on file and show the person is free of communicable disease and able to perform the job. Content and frequency: (1) Physical examination: before first resident contact, then periodically as set in the procedures below. The examination is done by a physician, advanced practice nurse or physician assistant and includes health history, review of systems, a statement of the person's ability to perform the essential job functions, and a statement that the person has no communicable disease. (2) Tuberculosis: baseline tuberculin skin test or blood test (IGRA) before first resident contact, then annual symptom screening and retesting after exposure or when symptoms develop. (3) Immunizations: documented immunity or vaccination for measles, mumps, rubella, varicella, tetanus/diphtheria/pertussis, and hepatitis B (offered), plus annual influenza vaccine (offered) and COVID-19 vaccine as recommended by DOH and CDC. The same requirements apply to contract and agency staff, whose employer or agency must supply proof or [AGENCY NAME] obtains it before the person works in the facility. The Administrator verifies the schedule against current DOH and CDC guidance at each annual manual review. Employees with occupational exposure to blood or other potentially infectious materials are offered hepatitis B vaccination at no cost under 29 CFR 1910.1030. Records of physical examinations are kept in the personnel file as required by N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.7(a)6 (see STF-05).

definitions.definition: A tuberculin skin test (TST) or an interferon-gamma release assay (IGRA) blood test used to detect latent or active tuberculosis infection.
Any individual who provides direct resident care in the facility through a contract, staffing agency or written agreement and is not an employee.
Reasonably anticipated contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials during assigned duties (29 CFR 1910.1030).
The written statement from the examining provider that the person is free of communicable disease and able to perform the job.

procedures: The conditional offer of employment, or contract with an agency, states that resident contact cannot begin until the health requirements below are met.
The new hire is given the employee health form and instructions. The examining provider completes the history, examination and health clearance statement.
The examination must be dated within 90 days before the start date. If it is older, the person is re-examined before first resident contact.

The Administrator or designee reviews the health clearance. If the provider notes any restriction, the Administrator decides in writing, with the RN's input, whether the person can safely do the job, and documents any accommodation.

Baseline TB screening is completed before first resident contact: a single TST read within 48 to 72 hours, or an IGRA. [AGENCY NAME] may accept a documented TB test result within the past 12 months if the written result and date are provided. A person with a previous positive test provides the result and a chest X-ray report plus a symptom screen.

A positive TB test result, or any TB symptom (cough over three weeks, fever, night sweats, weight loss), is referred immediately to the employee's provider and the local health department. The person does not work with residents until a provider clears them in writing.

The Administrator conducts a TB symptom screen each year with every employee and contract caregiver, documented on the annual health screening form. A repeat test is done after any known exposure or as directed by DOH or the local health department.
The employee updates the physical examination at least every 2 years, and sooner if there is a change in health status, a prolonged illness, or a return from leave following a communicable disease.

Immunization records are reviewed at hire: documented immunity for measles, mumps, rubella and varicella by vaccination record or titer, and a current tetanus/diphtheria/pertussis vaccination. Missing items are offered through the employee's provider.

Hepatitis B vaccination is offered, at no cost to the employee, within 10 working days of initial assignment to any employee with occupational exposure. An employee who declines signs a declination statement and may change their mind at any time.

Influenza vaccine is offered each year before influenza season. An employee who declines signs a declination, and may be asked to wear a mask during influenza season per infection control policy (SAF-07).
COVID-19 and any other vaccine recommended by DOH or CDC for health care workers are offered according to current guidance. The Administrator updates this policy when guidance changes.

Employees must report to the Administrator before working any symptoms of a communicable disease, such as fever, vomiting, diarrhea, rash or a draining wound. The Administrator or RN decides whether the employee stays home or is restricted, following SAF-07.

After a needlestick, splash or other exposure, the employee reports it at once, receives post-exposure evaluation and follow-up from a licensed provider at no cost, and the event is recorded as an incident (SAF-02). Post-exposure follow-up is documented in a confidential medical record under 29 CFR 1910.1030.

For contract and agency staff, the Administrator obtains a written attestation or copies of the physical examination, TB result and immunizations before the first shift. The agreement with the agency requires it to keep these current.

All health records are placed in a confidential section of the personnel file, separate from other employment records, and are available to DOH on request (STF-05). Bloodborne exposure and vaccination records are kept for the duration of employment plus 30 years under 29 CFR 1910.1030 and 29 CFR 1910.1020.

The Administrator maintains a health requirements tracking log with due dates for each person. The log is reviewed monthly and any overdue item results in removal of the person from the schedule until it is cured.
The Administrator reviews this policy at the annual manual review (GOV-05) and after any outbreak, and reports outbreak or communicable disease events as required by SAF-02 and REC-02.

responsibilities.duty: Enforces the no-clearance-no-resident-contact rule, reviews health clearances, maintains the tracking log and decides on restrictions.
Advises on work restrictions, infection control follow-up and exposure management.
Complete required examinations, tests and immunization documentation on time and report symptoms and exposures promptly.
Collects documents, files them in the confidential health section and updates the tracking log.

documentation: Pre-employment physical examination form with health clearance statement
Baseline TB test result and annual TB symptom screening forms
Immunization records, titers and signed declination forms
Hepatitis B offer and declination
Exposure incident reports and post-exposure follow-up (confidential)
Contract/agency staff health attestations
Health requirements tracking log

policies.title: Personnel Records
policies.applies_to: All employees; applicable parts apply to contract caregivers
policies.purpose: To keep a complete, accurate and secure personnel record for every employee, as required by N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.7(a)6, so that credentials and training can be verified and DOH can review them at any time.
policies.policy: This policy meets N.J.A.C. 8:36-5.7(a)6, which requires policies and procedures for the maintenance of personnel records for each employee, including at least name, previous employment, educational background, credentials, license number with effective date and date of expiration (if applicable), certification (if applicable), verification of credentials, records of physical examinations, job description, records of orientation and inservice education, and evaluation of job performance. [AGENCY NAME] keeps a personnel file for every employee that contains each of those items. The file also holds criminal history background check and registry results and PCA and CMA certification dates, renewals and continuing education (N.J.A.C. 8:36-9.1). Personnel files are kept secure, are confidential, and are available to DOH representatives on request.

definitions.definition: The record, paper or electronic, kept for each employee containing the items listed in this policy.
Documented confirmation, from the issuing authority or its registry, that a license or certification is valid and current.
A separate, restricted part of the file for medical examinations, immunization and exposure records.
